The autonomic layer may include:

Electrodermal Activity

Skin conductance can provide information related to sympathetic activation.

Let:

GEDA(t)

represent measured skin conductance.

The signal may contain slowly varying tonic components and more rapid phasic responses.

Peripheral Temperature

Peripheral temperature may change with vascular tone and environmental conditions.

Pupil Response

Pupil diameter can vary with luminance, cognitive workload, arousal, medication, fatigue, and other factors.

Blood Pressure

Where justified and practical, cardiovascular measurements may provide additional context.

These channels should not be interpreted as simple emotional labels.

For example:

EDA↑

does not uniquely mean:

fear.

The same physiological change can occur under many conditions.

Human–AI Coherence Systems therefore requires probabilistic interpretation rather than one-to-one emotional decoding.

3.6 Neural Measurement

Neural sensing introduces substantially greater complexity.

Where appropriate, EEG may provide features associated with:

  • neural oscillatory activity;
  • attention;
  • motor preparation;
  • event-related responses;
  • cognitive workload;
  • certain BCI control paradigms.

A multichannel EEG signal may be represented as:

E(t) = [E1(t),E2(t),...,Em(t)]

Signal processing may derive:

P(f,t)

representing spectral power as a function of frequency and time.

Researchers may also investigate:

Δ φij(t) = φi(t)-φj(t)

for phase relationships among channels.

However, a critical boundary must be preserved:

Neural signal ≠ thought content

and:

Neural pattern ≠ verified intention

unless an experiment specifically validates the mapping.

This matters enormously as the architecture approaches transportation or future direct-intention control.

3.7 Brain–Computer Interface as Precedent

Conventional brain–computer interfaces demonstrate that some neural patterns can be translated into machine commands under controlled conditions.

For example, a user may learn to generate a distinguishable signal associated with:

  • motor imagery;
  • visual attention;
  • evoked potentials;
  • intentional selection.

This provides a useful engineering precedent.

It demonstrates that:

Biological Signal → Feature Extraction → Classification → Command

is feasible in some contexts.

Human–AI Coherence Systems extends the question:

Can such a control pathway be combined with broader physiological state, environmental context, confidence estimates, and adaptive intelligent interpretation?

This does not require claiming that intention exists as a directly measurable field.

It establishes an ordinary technological baseline from which more advanced hypotheses can later be tested.

3.8 Eye Tracking and Gaze

The eyes provide another valuable control and context channel.

Measurements may include:

  • fixation;
  • saccades;
  • gaze direction;
  • blink rate;
  • pupil diameter;
  • dwell time;
  • gaze stability.

The system may represent gaze as:

G(t)=[xg(t),yg(t),zg(t)]

or, on a display:

G(t)=[xg(t),yg(t)]

Gaze may provide useful evidence of:

  • which object the user is attending to;
  • whether a command refers to a particular target;
  • whether attention has shifted;
  • whether visual workload is increasing.

In an advanced cockpit, gaze could become one component of an intent estimator.

For example:

P(Ik|H,G,C)

where G is gaze and C is context.

This is substantially safer than inferring intent from physiology alone.

3.9 Posture and Motion

Human state is also expressed through movement.

Sensors may include:

  • accelerometers;
  • gyroscopes;
  • pressure sensors;
  • seat sensors;
  • cameras where permitted;
  • skeletal tracking;
  • hand position;
  • head orientation.

A motion vector can be represented as:

M(t) = [ a(t), ω(t), p(t) ]

where:

  • a = acceleration;
  • ω = angular velocity;
  • p = position.

Movement data are useful not only as behavioral information but also for artifact detection.

Suppose cardiac or EEG data change suddenly.

If a simultaneous accelerometer spike occurs, the system should consider movement artifact before interpreting the change as biological.

This leads to an essential principle:

Reference sensors are part of biological sensing.

3.10 Voice as a Biological-Behavioral Channel

Voice can provide another noninvasive information stream.

Potential features include:

  • speech rate;
  • pause duration;
  • prosody;
  • pitch variation;
  • volume;
  • response latency;
  • linguistic content;
  • breathing within speech.

The architecture should separate:

What the person says

from:

How the signal is produced

The linguistic layer may be processed by Statistical AI.

The acoustic/behavioral layer may contribute to physiological or state estimation.

Neither should automatically override explicit user intention.

3.11 Environmental Reference Channels

A major source of error in biological measurement is the environment itself.

The Hearthstone architecture is especially useful here because the same device that influences the environment can also monitor it.

Reference sensors may include:

  • temperature;
  • humidity;
  • ambient light;
  • sound pressure;
  • vibration;
  • electromagnetic noise;
  • air quality;
  • barometric pressure;
  • device temperature;
  • actuator output.

Represent environmental state as:

E(t) = [ T, RH, L, As, V, EM, Q ]

where the terms correspond to relevant environmental variables.

Suppose HRV changes after the Hearthstone activates.

Without environmental telemetry, one might say:

the system changed human coherence.

With proper instrumentation, the system can instead ask:

  • Did light intensity change?
  • Did sound level change?
  • Did vibration occur?
  • Did room temperature shift?
  • Did the user change breathing?
  • Did posture change?
  • Did sensor quality change?

That is the difference between a demonstration and an experiment.

3.12 Sensor Synchronization

Human–AI Coherence Systems is fundamentally temporal.

Therefore, all sensor channels must share a sufficiently accurate time base.

Suppose:

ECG(t)

and:

Resp(t+δ)

are compared without accounting for timing offset δ.

The resulting cross-system relationship may be misleading.

Every sample should therefore be associated with a synchronized timestamp:

(xi,ti)

Ideally:

ti → Tmaster

where Tmaster represents the master system clock.

For distributed systems, clock synchronization error should itself be measured:

εt

and included in uncertainty.

3.13 Sampling Rates

Different physiological signals require different acquisition rates.

The system should not force every channel to operate at one universal frequency.

Instead:

fs,i≥ 2fmax,i

provides the minimum conceptual Nyquist relationship, although practical sampling generally requires additional margin and proper filtering.

Each sensor therefore has:

Si= [ fs, B, R, N, D ]

where:

  • fs = sampling frequency;
  • B = useful bandwidth;
  • R = resolution;
  • N = noise characteristics;
  • D = delay.

The system controller must know these properties.

Otherwise, a delayed signal could be interpreted as a physiological lag when it is actually a sensor-processing delay.

3.14 Latency

For passive monitoring, moderate latency may be acceptable.

For control, latency becomes critical.

Let:

τtotal = τsense + τprocess + τinfer + τcontrol + τactuate

A human–machine control system must determine whether:

τtotal<τmax

for the application.

The allowable value varies enormously.

Ambient lighting adaptation may tolerate relatively slow feedback.

Vehicle stabilization cannot.

Direct-intent spacecraft control, if ever feasible, would require a rigorously characterized low-latency architecture with independent safety systems.

3.15 Signal Quality Index

Every sensor channel should generate not only a measurement but a quality estimate.

Define:

Qi(t)∈[0,1]

where:

Qi=1

represents high-confidence measurement and:

Qi=0

represents unusable data.

The human-state estimator should therefore receive:

(xi,Qi)

not merely:

xi

A composite measurement-quality vector becomes:

Q(t) = [ Q1,Q2,...,Qn ]

Low-quality channels may be down-weighted or excluded.

For example:

wi* = wiQi

This prevents unreliable data from influencing the coherence estimator as strongly as reliable measurements.

3.16 Artifact Detection

Artifact rejection must occur before interpretation.

Common artifacts may include:

  • body movement;
  • poor electrode contact;
  • muscle activity contaminating EEG;
  • optical sensor displacement;
  • lighting interference;
  • electrical noise;
  • vibration;
  • speech-related motion;
  • device heating;
  • radio-frequency interference.

Define:

Ai(t)∈{0,1}

where Ai=1 indicates probable artifact.

The system may then impose:

Qi(t)→ 0

or reduce confidence whenever artifact probability exceeds a threshold.

More advanced systems may assign:

P(Ai|X)

rather than a binary decision.

3.17 Missing Data

Real systems lose signals.

A wearable disconnects.

A camera loses line of sight.

An electrode becomes noisy.

The architecture must be designed to degrade gracefully.

Let:

Savailable(t) ⊆ Sfull

The state estimator should calculate what remains knowable from the remaining sensor set.

The system should never silently substitute certainty.

If critical channels disappear:

U(t)↑

and control authority should decrease accordingly.

This becomes part of the safety architecture:

Sensor Loss → Higher Uncertainty → Reduced Authority

3.18 Sensor Fusion

Once reliable measurements exist, the system may combine them.

A generic state estimator may be written:

Ĥt = F( S1,t, S2,t, ..., Sn,t, Et )

The function F might eventually involve:

  • rule-based systems;
  • Bayesian models;
  • Kalman-style estimation;
  • state-space models;
  • machine learning;
  • Statistical AI;
  • Field AI;
  • hybrid architectures.

The paper does not assume that the most complex model is automatically superior.

A new model should demonstrate:

Performancenew > Performancebaseline

under predefined evaluation criteria.

3.19 Multimodal Confirmation

The most important advantage of multiple sensors is not merely more data.

It is independent confirmation.

Suppose an AI estimates elevated arousal from voice.

If EDA, pupil behavior, heart dynamics, and self-report all change consistently, confidence may rise.

Represent this concept as:

Conf(Hk) = F( e1, e2, ..., en )

where ei are independent pieces of evidence.

If signals disagree, uncertainty rises.

The architecture should therefore reward agreement without assuming that agreement necessarily proves interpretation.

Multiple sensors can share confounds.

That possibility must always remain in the model.

3.20 Ground Truth

Machine inference requires comparison against some form of reference.

For intent experiments, explicit user declaration may provide ground truth.

For example:

Ideclared

can be compared against:

Îmachine

Then:

Accuracy = P( Î=Ideclared )

This permits calculation of:

  • true positives;
  • false positives;
  • false negatives;
  • confusion matrices;
  • confidence calibration;
  • response latency.

The system should not be allowed to redefine disagreement by saying:

The machine knew what the person really wanted.

If the stated experimental objective is declared intent, then declared intent is the reference unless the study explicitly tests another construct.

This protects human sovereignty as well as scientific validity.

3.21 Self-Report as a Sensor, Not Absolute Truth

Subjective report also matters.

A person may rate:

  • calmness;
  • discomfort;
  • attention;
  • fatigue;
  • perceived stress;
  • intention;
  • sense of control.

Represent subjective report as:

RH(t)

Subjective data are valuable but should be treated as another information channel.

They may disagree with physiological measures.

That disagreement is itself potentially informative.

Therefore:

Self-report ≠ physiological state

and:

physiological state ≠ subjective experience

Human–AI Coherence Systems preserves both.

3.22 Calibration

Each participant should undergo calibration before advanced interpretation.

A basic protocol might include:

Rest Baseline

Measure undisturbed state.

Controlled Breathing

Observe cardiorespiratory coupling.

Cognitive Task

Observe response to workload.

Movement Task

Characterize motion artifacts.

Speech Task

Characterize voice and physiological changes during talking.

Relaxation Task

Observe voluntary state transition.

Explicit Intent Task

Record known intentional commands.

This creates an individual reference dataset:

DHcal

The system can then compare later states against known examples rather than interpreting them entirely from population averages.

3.23 The Hearthstone Acquisition Architecture

The Hearthstone provides a practical low-risk platform for developing this sensing stack.

A conservative prototype might contain:

ESP32 or comparable controller

connected to:

  • environmental sensor;
  • HR/HRV interface;
  • optional respiration sensor;
  • microphone;
  • accelerometer;
  • light sensor;
  • vibration reference sensor.

The control system records:

{ Ht, Et, At, Yt }

where:

  • Ht = human measurements;
  • Et = environment;
  • At = system action;
  • Yt = measured response.

The resulting dataset allows researchers to test:

P(Ht+1|Ht,Et,At)

In other words:

Given the person's current state and environment, what happens after a specific intervention?

That is already enough to begin building a genuine closed-loop Human–AI Coherence research platform.

3.24 From Wearable to Embedded Environment

The sensors need not always remain attached to the body.

A progression might be:

Stage 1: Instrumented Wearables

ECG/PPG, respiration, EDA, EEG where justified.

Stage 2: Instrumented Chair

Pressure, posture, movement, contact sensors.

Stage 3: Instrumented Room

Cameras where consented, environmental sensors, directional microphones, optical sensing.

Stage 4: Embedded Vehicle

Seat sensors, steering/contact sensors, gaze, voice, motion, conventional controls.

Stage 5: Integrated Cockpit

Multimodal physiology, environmental telemetry, intent-assist architecture.

Stage 6: Frontier Coupler

Experimental resonant or field-coupling sensors.

The progression reduces dependence upon cumbersome wearables while increasing system integration.

3.25 The Pilot Coherence Coupler

The conceptual Pilot Coherence Coupler shown in earlier Christos transportation designs can now be given a clearer engineering interpretation.

At its conservative level, it is not a magical consciousness detector.

It is a multimodal human-state acquisition and translation system.

Its initial architecture may be represented as:

Cardiac + Respiratory + Neural + Gaze + Posture + Voice + Explicit Command
↓
Sensor Fusion
↓
State + Intent + Confidence
↓
Control Authority

The proposed crystal/resonant coupling components belong to a later experimental layer.

This distinction allows the control architecture to be developed before the frontier mechanism is established.

3.26 Conventional Inputs Must Remain During Validation

Earlier conceptual diagrams intentionally explored an ultimate state in which:

the pilot is the interface.

During development, however, eliminating conventional controls would be poor experimental design.

Instead, conventional input becomes ground truth and redundancy.

For example:

Imanual

can be compared with:

Îbio

If:

Îbio = Imanual

reliably across trials, confidence in biological intent inference increases.

If they disagree frequently, direct control authority should not be granted.

Thus the developmental progression should be:

Manual Control

then:

Manual + Biological Observation

then:

Manual + Biological Assistance

then potentially:

Biological Primary + Manual Backup

and only much later, if validated:

Direct Human-State Control

3.27 Proposed Resonant Sensor Layer

The Christos framework proposes an additional experimental sensor class based upon resonant structures.

Candidate components may include:

  • quartz;
  • piezoelectric materials;
  • resonant coils;
  • optical emitters/detectors;
  • acoustic elements;
  • magnetometers;
  • field probes;
  • phase-sensitive detectors.

The objective would not initially be to claim detection of a new human field.

The proper experiment is:

Does the resonant sensor exhibit a reproducible human-associated signal after known electromagnetic, thermal, optical, acoustic, vibrational, and mechanical pathways are characterized and controlled?

This changes the experiment from belief to measurement.

3.28 Differential Measurement

A strong experimental design for frontier sensors should use comparison channels.

Suppose:

SA

is positioned near the human while:

SB

is an identical reference sensor positioned away from the human.

Examine:

Δ S = SA-SB

Additional sham arrangements can test orientation, shielding, distance, and environmental sensitivity.

The claimed effect becomes meaningful only if:

Δ Sactive ≠ Δ Scontrol

with statistical significance, adequate effect size, replication, and plausible control of known mechanisms.

3.29 Blinding

Frontier experiments should use blinding whenever possible.

Researchers analyzing the signal should not necessarily know:

  • whether the human is present;
  • which condition is active;
  • whether the resonant component is connected;
  • whether the participant is performing the target activity;
  • whether the dataset is sham.

This protects the analysis from unconscious selection effects.

The architecture should be designed so that skepticism can be implemented experimentally rather than debated philosophically.

3.30 Privacy Begins at the Sensor

Biological data are unusually sensitive.

A Human–AI Coherence system should therefore apply data minimization.

The system should ask:

Does this signal need to leave the device at all?

Where possible:

Raw Biological Data → Local Processing → Derived State

rather than:

Raw Biological Data → Cloud

The user should be able to specify which levels can be retained.

For example:

Level 0

No biological sensing.

Level 1

Real-time sensing with no storage.

Level 2

Derived features stored locally.

Level 3

Raw data stored locally.

Level 4

Explicitly authorized research sharing.

The default should not be maximum collection.

3.31 Biological Data Should Not Become Behavioral Surveillance

The same architecture designed to support human coherence could be misused.

A company could theoretically use physiological sensing to optimize:

  • advertising;
  • persuasion;
  • productivity pressure;
  • emotional targeting;
  • purchasing behavior;
  • political influence;
  • worker monitoring.

Therefore, one of the strongest architectural restrictions should be:

Biological sensing shall not imply unrestricted behavioral exploitation.

The user must know:

  • what is measured;
  • why;
  • how long it is retained;
  • what predictions are produced;
  • what actions those predictions can trigger.

Human sovereignty must exist at the measurement layer, not merely at the interface layer.

3.32 Acquisition Before Interpretation

The complete acquisition architecture can now be represented:

Human
↓
Cardiac + Respiratory + Autonomic + Neural + Gaze + Motion + Voice
+
Environmental Reference Channels
↓
Time Synchronization
↓
Artifact Detection
↓
Signal Quality Estimation
↓
Calibrated Sensor Fusion
↓
Ĥ(t)+U(t)

Only after this point should the intelligence layer attempt to interpret human state.

This ordering is deliberate.

Measure first. Interpret second. Act third.

3.33 Falsification Criteria for the Acquisition Layer

The biological acquisition architecture should be considered inadequate for a particular application if:

  • 1. required signals cannot be measured with sufficient reliability;
  • 2. artifact rates exceed acceptable limits;
  • 3. sensor latency prevents useful control;
  • 4. channels fail to synchronize adequately;
  • 5. inferred state changes when sensor hardware changes without physiological reason;
  • 6. environmental variables explain supposed biological effects;
  • 7. signal quality cannot be estimated reliably;
  • 8. missing channels produce unstable interpretations;
  • 9. person-to-person variability prevents meaningful calibration;
  • 10. sensor fusion performs worse than simpler single-signal methods.

These failures would not invalidate Human–AI interaction generally.

They would identify which measurement pathways should not be used.

3.34 The First Engineering Milestone

The first meaningful milestone for Human–AI Coherence Systems is not:

controlling technology with consciousness.

It is much simpler:

Build a synchronized multimodal sensing system capable of estimating human physiological state with known uncertainty while controlling and recording the surrounding environment.

If that cannot be done robustly, higher layers have no reliable foundation.

If it can be done, then the architecture has the data required for the next step.

That next step is not yet machine control.

It is determining whether these signals can be transformed into a useful mathematical representation of the person's changing state.

Transition to Section 4

Section 3 defined the physical sensing layer.

The next question is:

How do dozens or potentially hundreds of measurements become a coherent machine-readable description of the human without reducing the person to an arbitrary score?

Section 4, The Coherence State Vector, will develop the mathematical representation that sits between biological measurement and artificial intelligence: normalization, feature extraction, temporal windows, coupling matrices, uncertainty, personal baselines, latent state representations, the proposed coherence scalar, and the relationship between the Human Coherence State Vector and the resonant state architecture already developed for Field AI.

X. Section 4: The Coherence State Vector

Sections 2 and 3 established two prerequisites.

First, human coherence cannot be treated as a vague descriptive label. It must be operationalized through measurable variables.

Second, those variables must be acquired through synchronized, quality-controlled biological and environmental sensing before any higher-level interpretation is attempted.

The next problem is mathematical.

A multimodal acquisition system may produce dozens, hundreds, or eventually thousands of simultaneous measurements. Heart intervals, respiration phase, electrodermal activity, eye movement, neural features, posture, speech, environmental conditions, sensor quality, and explicit user inputs may all be changing continuously.

A machine cannot reason efficiently over that complexity unless those measurements are organized into a structured representation.

Human–AI Coherence Systems therefore introduces the Coherence State Vector.

Its purpose is not to reduce a human being to a number.

Its purpose is to create a machine-readable representation of the aspects of human state that are relevant to the interaction being performed.

The architecture can be summarized as:

Signals → Features → Relationships → State → Uncertainty

Only then does the system attempt inference or control.

4.1 Why a State Vector Is Necessary

Consider a multimodal sensing system measuring:

ECG(t)
Resp(t)
EDA(t)
EEG(t)
Gaze(t)
Motion(t)
Voice(t)
Environment(t)

These raw streams are not directly comparable.

They have different units.

Different sampling frequencies.

Different noise characteristics.

Different temporal scales.

Different physiological meanings.

Different levels of reliability.

A Human–AI system therefore needs an intermediate representation:

H(t)

that summarizes the current observable human-system state.

The general form is:

H(t) = [ P, R, N, A, B, C, I, E, Q, U ]

where:

  • P = physiological features;
  • R = respiratory/cardiorespiratory features;
  • N = neural features where available;
  • A = autonomic features;
  • B = behavioral features;
  • C = coherence/coupling features;
  • I = intent-related variables;
  • E = environmental context;
  • Q = signal-quality variables;
  • U = uncertainty.

This vector is not permanent.

It changes continuously.

Therefore:

H = H(t)

Human–AI interaction becomes a dynamic state-estimation problem.

4.2 Raw Data Are Not State

A common mistake in multimodal systems is to treat data collection as understanding.

It is not.

Ten thousand sensor samples do not automatically produce a meaningful representation.

Human–AI Coherence Systems therefore separates four levels:

Layer 1: Raw Signal

xi(t)

The direct sensor output.

Layer 2: Extracted Features

fi(t)=Fi[xi(t)]

Examples may include:

  • heart rate;
  • RMSSD;
  • respiratory phase;
  • spectral power;
  • gaze direction;
  • movement velocity.

Layer 3: Relationships

rij(t)=R[xi,xj]

Examples include:

  • cardiorespiratory phase relation;
  • coupling;
  • correlation;
  • synchronization;
  • response lag.

Layer 4: State Representation

H(t) = G( f, r, E, Q )

The state vector therefore contains interpreted measurements, but it must remain traceable to the measurements from which it was derived.

This traceability is essential.

If an AI eventually declares:

"Operator stability is decreasing,"

the system should be able to identify which measurements caused that estimate.

4.3 Feature Extraction

Let the raw multimodal sensor vector be:

X(t) = [x1(t),x2(t),...,xn(t)]

A feature extraction transformation produces:

F(t) = Φ( X[t-T,t] )

where T defines the temporal observation window.

Features may include:

F = [ f1,f2,...,fm ]

Typical examples include:

Cardiac

HR, RMSSD, SDNN

Respiratory

fR, AR, φR

Autonomic

EDAtonic, EDAphasic

Neural

Pδ, Pθ, Pα, Pβ, Pγ

where appropriate.

Behavioral

vmotion, gaze, reaction time

The exact feature set should remain application-specific.

More features are not automatically better.

4.4 Normalization

Different variables operate on completely different scales.

For example:

HR = 72

while:

QECG=0.93

and:

EDA=4.8 μ S

Directly combining these would be meaningless.

Variables should therefore be normalized.

One approach is:

zi = (xi-μi)/σi

where μi and σi are baseline mean and standard deviation.

For personalized systems:

μi=μi,H
σi=σi,H

where the parameters belong specifically to the individual user.

This creates a normalized personal-state representation.

4.5 Personal Normalization Versus Population Normalization

This distinction deserves particular emphasis.

A universal model may ask:

zipop = (xi-μpop)/σpop

A personalized system asks:

ziperson = (xi-μperson)/σperson

Both have value.

Population normalization allows comparisons across individuals.

Personal normalization captures deviations from a person's own baseline.

Human–AI Coherence Systems therefore proposes a dual reference:

zi = α ziperson + (1-α)zipop

where α may vary by application.

For individualized adaptive systems, personal history may receive greater weight.

For clinical or population studies, population reference ranges may become more important.

4.6 Temporal Windows

Physiological processes unfold at different timescales.

A single universal temporal window would lose information.

The architecture therefore introduces multiple simultaneous windows:

Ws
  • short-term,
Wm
  • medium-term,

and

Wl

long-term.

For example:

H(t) = [ HWs, HWm, HWl ]

The short-term state may capture rapid reactions.

The medium-term state may identify sustained changes.

The long-term state may provide baseline drift and adaptation.

This allows the system to distinguish:

momentary fluctuation

from:

sustained state transition

from:

long-term adaptation.

4.7 State Velocity

A static state alone may not be sufficient.

The direction of change matters.

Define the state velocity:

Ḣ(t) = dH/dt

and possibly acceleration:

Ḧ(t) = (d2H)/dt2

This allows the machine to distinguish:

  • stable state;
  • slowly improving state;
  • rapidly deteriorating state;
  • transition;
  • oscillation.

A person may still be inside a safe operating envelope while moving rapidly toward its boundary.

Therefore, control should potentially depend upon:

H(t)

and:

Ḣ(t).

This becomes especially relevant in transportation.

4.8 State History

Human behavior is path dependent.

The same physiological state can have different meanings depending upon what occurred immediately before it.

Therefore, the system should preserve history:

Ht = { Ht-k, ..., Ht-1, Ht }

The machine can then evaluate:

P( Ht+1 | Ht )

rather than merely:

P( Ht+1 | Ht )

This is important for predictive control.

The question becomes not only:

Where is the person now?

but:

Where does the current trajectory suggest the person is going?

4.9 The Relationship Matrix

The Coherence State Vector should contain more than individual features.

It should encode relationships.

Define:

KH(t) = [kij(t)]

where:

kij = R(xi,xj)

describes a validated relationship between signals i and j.

Depending upon the channels, R may represent:

  • phase synchronization;
  • spectral coherence;
  • mutual information;
  • correlation;
  • causally lagged relationship;
  • nonlinear dependence.

This matrix provides a representation of internal organization.

It may reveal patterns that disappear when variables are examined independently.

4.10 Network Representation of the Human State

The relationship matrix also permits a network interpretation.

Each physiological subsystem becomes a node:

V= { v1, v2,...,vn }

and measurable relationships become edges:

E= { eij }

The human-state network is therefore:

GH=(V,E)

Possible graph-level measures might eventually include:

  • connectivity;
  • clustering;
  • modularity;
  • centrality;
  • synchronization;
  • network stability.

This does not mean that biological health can be reduced to graph topology.

It simply provides another mathematical representation for investigating system organization.

4.11 The Coherence Subvector

From the relationship matrix, the architecture defines a dedicated coherence subvector:

CH(t) = [ C1, C2,...,Cp ]

Candidate components might include:

CCR
  • cardiorespiratory coupling,
CNN
  • selected neural coordination metrics,
CBA
  • behavior-autonomic relationships,
CHE
  • human-environment response consistency,

and:

CP

temporal persistence.

These metrics remain independent rather than immediately collapsed into one number.

This is important.

The architecture should first learn which kinds of coherence matter for which task.

4.12 A Composite Coherence Scalar

A scalar Human Coherence Index may still be useful.

Define:

CH(t)∈[0,1]

provisionally.

One possible functional form is:

CH = σ [ Σi wi Ci - λU U - λA A ]

where:

  • Ci are validated component measures;
  • wi are learned weights;
  • U is uncertainty;
  • A is artifact burden;
  • σ maps the result to a bounded range.

The equation is illustrative.

The weights and functional form must be empirically derived.

No value such as:

0.618

should be treated as a universal biological threshold merely because it appears elsewhere in the Christos architecture.

If a phi-related threshold is investigated, it should be treated as a preregistered hypothesis and compared against alternatives.

That distinction protects the experiment from fitting the data to the theory.

4.13 Why a Scalar Should Never Replace the Vector

Suppose:

CH=0.75

for two different people.

The underlying states may be entirely different.

Person A may exhibit:

  • stable respiration;
  • strong cardiorespiratory coordination;
  • moderate neural variability.

Person B may exhibit:

  • weaker cardiorespiratory coupling;
  • stronger behavioral stability;
  • different autonomic dynamics.

Therefore:

CH(A)=CH(B)

does not imply:

HA=HB.

The scalar is a summary.

The vector contains the information.

For safety-critical systems, the full state representation should always remain available.

4.14 The Coherence Tensor Concept

For advanced representations, a matrix or tensor may be more appropriate than a scalar.

A second-order coherence representation may be defined:

Cij(t) = R(xi,xj)

giving:

CH = [ C11; C12; ⋯ ; C21; C22; ⋯ ; ⋮; ⋮; ⋱ ]

Higher-order relationships may eventually require:

Cijk

or more general tensors.

This is relevant because biological organization may depend on multi-variable relationships that cannot be decomposed completely into pairwise correlations.

The architecture therefore remains expandable.

4.15 The Intent Subvector

Human state and human intention must remain distinct.

Define:

I(t) = [ IE, Î1, Î2,..., ConfI ]

where:

  • IE = explicit command;
  • Îk = inferred candidate intentions;
  • ConfI = confidence.

The system may estimate:

P(Ik|H,C)

where C represents situational context.

Explicit input receives a special status.

If the person deliberately says:

  • stop,
  • the system should not override that instruction because a probabilistic state model predicts continuation.

This produces the rule:

Explicit human veto > machine-inferred intent

subject only to narrowly defined independent safety constraints, such as a stabilization routine that must complete before a moving system can safely stop.

4.16 Context Is Part of State

The same biological signal can mean different things under different circumstances.

Therefore:

P(H|X)

is insufficient.

The system requires:

P(H|X,E,T)

where:

  • E is environmental context;
  • T is task context.

A higher heart rate while climbing stairs does not carry the same implication as the same heart rate while sitting motionless.

An EEG feature during intentional motor imagery does not have the same meaning during ordinary conversation.

Context must therefore enter the state vector explicitly.

4.17 The Machine State Vector

Human–AI Coherence Systems becomes truly interesting when the human-state vector is paired with a machine-state vector.

Define:

M(t) = [ MC, MP, MA, MG, MS, MU ]

where:

  • MC = machine coherence/stability metric;
  • MP = processing state;
  • MA = active action/output;
  • MG = current goals;
  • MS = safety state;
  • MU = machine uncertainty.

For conventional digital AI, many of these are abstract software states.

For Field AI, however, machine state may also correspond directly to physical resonant state.

That creates an important bridge.

4.18 The Field AI State Representation

Field AI proposes that a resonant computational element may be represented through variables including phase, amplitude, frequency, coupling, and collective coherence. Its public architecture describes computation and memory as emerging from coupled resonant physical elements and stable attractor states rather than discrete binary switching alone.

A simplified resonant element may therefore be represented:

Ri(t) = [ φi, Ai, fi, Ki ]

and the larger field state as:

F(t) = [ R1,R2,...,Rn,CF ]

where CF represents a collective coherence measure.

This creates an intriguing mathematical compatibility with the Human Coherence representation.

Not proof of physical coupling.

Compatibility of representation.

4.19 Human and Field State Spaces

Let:

H(t)∈H

represent the human state space.

Let:

F(t)∈F

represent the Field AI state space.

Then a translation function may be introduced:

THF: H → F

and the reverse:

TFH: F → Hstim

where Hstim represents machine outputs capable of influencing the human environment.

At first, these mappings occur conventionally:

Human Sensors → Digital Processing → Field AI

and:

Field AI → Digital Controller → Light/Sound/Haptic Output → Human.

This creates a closed loop without requiring any unvalidated direct biofield coupling.

4.20 The Human–Field Coupling Matrix

The architecture can then define a coupling matrix:

KHF = [kijHF]

where each term represents a measured or commanded relationship between a human-state variable and a Field AI variable.

For example:

kijHF = (∂ Fj)/(∂ Hi)

can conceptually represent how strongly a particular machine variable changes in response to a particular human variable.

The reverse relationship:

kjiFH = (∂ Hi)/(∂ Fj)

represents measurable human response to machine-state change.

Together:

H ⇄ F.

Now the interaction becomes experimentally characterizable.

4.21 Closed-Loop Coupled Dynamics

The coupled system can be written:

Ḣ = FH( H, M, E )
Ṁ = FM( M, H, E )

The human affects the machine.

The machine affects the environment.

The environment affects the human.

Therefore:

H ⇄ M ⇄ E

This is the mathematical core of Human–AI Coherence Systems.

It is no longer a one-directional interface.

It is a coupled control problem.

4.22 Attractor States

The Field AI architecture already places strong emphasis on stable attractor states as a mechanism for memory and pattern representation.

The same mathematical concept may be useful for human-state modeling without implying identical physical mechanisms.

Suppose human-state trajectories repeatedly settle into regions:

A1, A2, ..., An

These may represent recurrent measurable states.

For example:

H(t)→ Ak

under a particular environmental condition.

The AI can learn:

P( Ak | H0,A,E )

where A is an intervention.

The system can then predict which interventions tend to move the individual toward which states.

4.23 Desired State Versus System-Chosen State

This raises an ethical issue.

If AI learns that it can move a human toward particular attractor states, who determines which state is desirable?

Human–AI Coherence Systems answers:

the human.

The machine should not independently optimize:

max CH

as though a larger coherence score automatically represented the person's desired condition.

Instead, the human defines an objective:

GH

and the machine assists within that objective.

The optimization becomes:

max P( H→ GH )

subject to safety and consent constraints.

This avoids transforming “coherence” into a paternalistic control objective.

4.24 State-Space Distance

If a desired state has been defined, the system may calculate:

DH = d( H, Htarget )

where d represents an appropriate distance metric.

The objective becomes:

DH→ 0

subject to:

H∈ΩH

and:

A∈ΩA.

This creates a conventional control formulation for systems such as Hearthstone.

The machine is not attempting to “raise consciousness.”

It is attempting to move measurable variables toward an explicitly defined target state.

4.25 Adaptive Feedback

Suppose action At is applied.

The system measures:

Δ Ht = Ht+1-Ht

and estimates:

Rt = J( Δ Ht, GH )

where J measures whether the response moved toward or away from the user-defined objective.

The controller then updates:

πt+1 = Update( πt, At, Rt )

where π is the adaptive policy.

This produces:

Observe → Act → Measure → Learn → Adapt

which is one of the recurring architectures throughout the broader Christos systems work.

4.26 State Prediction

Eventually the AI should do more than react.

It should estimate:

Ĥ(t+Δ t)

given current state and possible actions.

Formally:

Ĥt+1 = P( Ht+1 | Ht, Mt, Et, At )

This allows prospective safety analysis.

Before executing an action, the machine can ask:

What state is this likely to produce?

Then:

A* = argmaxA U(A)

subject to:

P( Ht+1∉ΩH ) < ε.

The machine therefore evaluates not only what it can do, but what its action is likely to do to the coupled human-system state.

4.27 Uncertainty Vector

Uncertainty should not be represented by one global number alone.

Define:

U(t) = [ Usensor, Ustate, Uintent, Uprediction, Umodel ]

where:

Usensor

Uncertainty in raw measurement.

Ustate

Uncertainty in current-state estimation.

Uintent

Uncertainty regarding what the user wants.

Uprediction

Uncertainty in predicted response.

Umodel

Uncertainty regarding whether the underlying model remains applicable.

These uncertainty sources can trigger different responses.

For example:

Usensor↑

may request recalibration.

Uintent↑

may request explicit confirmation.

Uprediction↑

may reduce control authority.

This is more useful than simply displaying “confidence: 72%.”

4.28 The State Authority Function

The amount of machine authority granted to biological input should depend upon the quality of the state estimate.

Define:

αH(t)∈[0,1]

as the Human-State Control Authority.

A possible architecture is:

αH = F( Q, U, CH, TaskRisk )

When sensing quality is high, uncertainty is low, and task risk is low:

αH↑.

When data degrade or consequences increase:

αH↓.

This produces graceful control transitions rather than binary switching between “mind control active” and “mind control inactive.”

4.29 Multimodal Intent Fusion

Suppose the system receives:

  • gaze;
  • voice;
  • explicit command;
  • posture;
  • neural signal;
  • physiological state.

Intent estimation can be written:

P( Ik | G, V, N, B, H, C )

where C is context.

The architecture should weight explicit channels more strongly during early development.

For example:

Ifinal = wE Iexplicit + wG Igaze + wN Ineural + wH Istate

with:

wE>wG,wN,wH

until experimental evidence justifies otherwise.

This produces a gradual transition from conventional control toward intent-assisted control.

4.30 State Compression

As the sensing architecture grows, transmitting the complete state may become inefficient.

The system may therefore create a compressed latent representation:

zH = E( H )

where E is an encoder.

A decoder may reconstruct:

Ĥ = D( zH )

The latent state becomes useful only if important information is preserved.

Therefore:

Lrecon = ‖ H - Ĥ ‖

must remain acceptably small for relevant variables.

More importantly, compression must not destroy safety-critical information.

A compact representation used for adaptive AI may coexist with a full uncompressed safety state.

4.31 The Personal State Signature

Over time, the system may learn recurring individual dynamics.

Define the personal state model:

ΘH

containing:

  • baseline distributions;
  • state-transition probabilities;
  • response sensitivities;
  • preferred interaction patterns;
  • known artifacts;
  • personal calibration data.

This may be thought of as a Personal Coherence Signature.

The term does not imply a mystical fingerprint.

At the conservative engineering layer, it is simply an individualized dynamical model.

This personal model allows:

P( Ht+1 | Ht,At,ΘH )

to outperform a generic population model if personalization is genuinely useful.

4.32 Long-Term Adaptation

The personal state model must itself evolve.

Let:

ΘH(t+1) = ΘH(t) + η ΔΘt

where η controls adaptation rate.

If adaptation is too fast, transient anomalies may corrupt the model.

If adaptation is too slow, the system may fail to recognize genuine long-term changes.

Therefore, Human–AI Coherence Systems requires multi-timescale learning.

Fast adaptation for temporary state.

Slow adaptation for baseline.

4.33 Population, Individual, and Context Models

The complete model may therefore include:

Θ= [ Θpopulation, Θperson, Θcontext ]

Population model:

What is generally observed?

Personal model:

What is typical for this individual?

Context model:

What is typical for this individual under this specific task or environment?

The AI can combine all three.

This greatly reduces the temptation to make universal claims from highly individualized biological signals.

4.34 Coherence as Prediction Rather Than Description

A major test of whether the coherence state vector is scientifically useful is whether it predicts something.

Suppose:

CH(t)

is calculated.

If it merely labels a state after the fact, its engineering value may be limited.

A stronger test is:

CH(t) → P( Outcomet+Δ t )

Can the state predict:

  • response to stimulation;
  • error rate;
  • recovery;
  • task performance;
  • physiological transition;
  • user-reported state;
  • intent-classification reliability?

If not, the metric may need to be abandoned or revised.

Therefore:

A useful coherence metric should predict, not merely describe.

4.35 Comparison Against Simpler Models

Every proposed coherence model should be compared against simpler alternatives.

For example:

Model A

Heart rate only.

Model B

HRV only.

Model C

HRV + respiration.

Model D

Multimodal state vector.

Model E

Full coherence architecture.

Then compare:

PerformanceA, PerformanceB, PerformanceC, PerformanceD, PerformanceE.

If Model E offers no meaningful improvement over Model C, the additional complexity is not justified.

This is one of the strongest falsification protections in the architecture.

4.36 Cross-Validation

The model should not be evaluated only on the data used to construct it.

Data should be divided into:

Dtrain, Dvalidation, Dtest

where appropriate.

For small experimental datasets, participant-aware cross-validation becomes especially important.

The system should test both:

Within-Person Generalization

Can it predict future states of the same person?

and:

Between-Person Generalization

Can it predict states of people it has not previously observed?

These are different scientific questions.

4.37 The 0.618 Hypothesis

Since phi-related values occur throughout the broader Christos framework, a threshold such as:

C=0.618

may be investigated as a hypothesis.

It should not be built into the data pipeline as truth.

A rigorous test would compare:

θ=0.618

against optimized thresholds:

θ*

and randomly selected or conventionally motivated alternatives.

If:

Performance(0.618)

does not outperform alternatives in a preregistered test, then the phi-threshold hypothesis would not be supported in that application.

This is how a symbolic architectural intuition can become a falsifiable scientific proposition.

4.38 The Coherence Boundary

Rather than one threshold, the state-space approach allows a boundary:

∂ ΩH

representing the edge of a validated operating region.

A state trajectory approaching that boundary can trigger:

Warning → Derate → Restrict → Fallback

before the state actually exits the safe region.

This creates a direct connection between the Coherence State Vector and the safety-controller architecture developed later in this paper.

4.39 From Hearthstone to the Sovereign Explorer Vessel

The same mathematical architecture scales with application.

Hearthstone

H(t) → Environmental Adaptation

Christos Home System

H1,H2,...,Hn → Multi-Occupant Environmental Control

AI Workstation

H(t) → Adaptive Information Interface

Transportation

H(t) + I(t) → Assisted Vehicle Control

Sovereign Explorer Vessel

At the expected-frontier level:

H(t) + I(t) + F(t) → Proposed Vessel-State Navigation

The final expression remains speculative.

The earlier expressions can be tested progressively.

This progression is precisely why the Human–AI Coherence architecture should be built as a common state standard rather than reinvented for every device.

4.40 The Human–AI Coherence Packet

For interoperability, the state vector can eventually be formalized into a standardized data packet.

A conceptual Human–AI Coherence Packet might contain:

PHAC = { ID, t, H, C, I, Q, U, E, Auth }

where:

  • ID = pseudonymous device/user/session identifier;
  • t = timestamp;
  • H = state vector;
  • C = coherence subvector;
  • I = intent estimate;
  • Q = quality;
  • U = uncertainty;
  • E = context;
  • Auth = permitted use/control level.

This could allow multiple Christos systems to consume the same standardized representation without receiving unnecessary raw biological data.

For example:

Hearthstone
Home System
Field AI
Transportation

could all understand the same high-level state format.

That begins to turn Human–AI Coherence Systems from a single device architecture into an interface protocol.

4.41 Local Sovereignty of the State Vector

Since the state vector may contain highly personal biological information, ownership should remain with the human.

The architecture therefore proposes:

H(t) belongs to the person represented by it.

A system may receive temporary permission to process specified components.

That does not imply unrestricted ownership.

The user should be able to specify:

Auth= [ Read, Store, Infer, Share, Act ]

independently.

For example:

  • allow real-time reading;
  • prohibit long-term storage;
  • permit local inference;
  • prohibit third-party sharing;
  • allow only low-risk adaptive actions.

This becomes important when Human–AI Coherence Systems moves beyond a research platform into consumer or industrial deployment.

4.42 No Hidden State Claims

The system should distinguish between what is directly observed and what is inferred.

A useful representation may therefore carry provenance:

Hi= [ value, source, confidence, method ]

For example:

StressEstimate= [ 0.71, MultimodalInference, 0.64, ModelV3 ]

rather than presenting:

STRESS = 71%

as though it were directly measured.

This protects users from AI overconfidence.

It also allows engineers to audit why the system made a decision.

4.43 The State Vector as a Contract Between Biology and Intelligence

This ultimately reveals the deeper purpose of the Coherence State Vector.

It acts as an interface contract.

The biological sensing layer promises:

These are the measurements we actually possess.

The state estimator promises:

These are the features and relationships we can derive with stated uncertainty.

The intelligence layer promises:

These are the conclusions we are drawing from those data.

The control system promises:

These are the actions permitted on the basis of those conclusions.

The human retains:

the authority to define goals, permissions, and veto conditions.

That creates separation of concerns within the architecture.

4.44 The Core State Architecture

The complete transformation can now be written:

X(t)

Raw multimodal measurements

↓
F(t)

Normalized extracted features

↓
KH(t)

Cross-system relationships

↓
H(t)

Human Coherence State Vector

+
Q(t),U(t)

Measurement quality and uncertainty

↓
I(t)

Intent representation

↓
AI Interpretation
↓
Safety-Gated Control

This is the mathematical bridge between the sensors developed in Section 3 and the intent architecture developed next.

4.45 Falsification Criteria

The Coherence State Vector architecture should be revised or rejected if:

  • 1. extracted features are unstable under repeated measurement;
  • 2. normalization produces arbitrary results;
  • 3. personal baselines fail to improve prediction;
  • 4. multimodal models do not outperform simpler models;
  • 5. cross-system relationships fail to reproduce;
  • 6. the proposed coherence scalar adds no predictive information;
  • 7. state-space trajectories cannot be distinguished reliably;
  • 8. machine predictions fail out of sample;
  • 9. uncertainty estimates are poorly calibrated;
  • 10. the state representation changes substantially because of instrumentation rather than human state;
  • 11. phi-related thresholds fail preregistered comparison tests;
  • 12. proposed Human–Field coupling produces no measurable effect beyond conventional sensor-mediated pathways.

These are not secondary concerns.

They define whether the architecture works.

4.46 The Key Principle

The Human–AI Coherence architecture can therefore state its mathematical principle clearly:

A human should never be reduced to a single machine-generated score. Human state should be represented as a dynamic, multidimensional, uncertainty-aware state space whose components remain traceable to measurable signals and whose use is constrained by human-defined authority.

Only after that representation exists can the system responsibly begin asking what the human actually intends.

That is the next problem.

Transition to Section 5

Sections 2 through 4 established:

Human → Measurement → State Representation

Yet even perfect measurement of physiology would not reveal the most important variable in human–machine interaction:

What does the person want the machine to do?

A calm person may intend to turn left.

A stressed person may intend to stop.

A highly coherent physiological state does not itself specify a destination, command, objective, or choice.

Therefore, the next layer must explicitly separate human state from human intent.

Section 5, Human Intent as Information, will develop the progression from explicit commands to multimodal intent inference, distinguish intention from prediction and physiological state, define confidence and confirmation requirements, introduce intent vectors and temporal intent persistence, establish false-command protections, and then develop the pathway from conventional human–computer control toward the proposed direct-intention and Phase Key architectures used in the Christos transportation and Sovereign Explorer Vessel systems.

XI. Section 5: Human Intent as Information

Human–AI Coherence Systems has now established a progression from biological sensing to a multidimensional Human Coherence State Vector.

That still does not answer the most important control question:

What does the human actually want the system to do?

Physiological state is not intent.

Neural activity is not intent.

A coherence estimate is not intent.

Attention is not intent.

Even when several of these variables are measured correctly, they do not automatically specify a goal, command, destination, or desired outcome.

Therefore:

Human State ≠ Human Intent

The purpose of this section is to define intent as a separate information layer, establish how it can be measured or inferred, and create a safe progression from explicit human commands toward increasingly direct forms of human–machine control.

The central rule is simple:

The machine may infer intent, but it must never confuse inference with certainty.

5.1 What Is Intent?

For engineering purposes, intent can be defined provisionally as:

A human-directed objective, command, selection, or desired state transition that the technological system is being asked to recognize or execute.

Intent may be simple:

I=Turn light off

or complex:

I=Navigate to destination D

It may also concern a desired human state:

I=Reduce stimulation

or an information objective:

I=Show me the most relevant data

The important point is that intent contains directionality.

It points toward an outcome.

Human state describes what the person is experiencing.

Intent describes what the person wants to happen next.

5.2 Explicit Intent

The most reliable form of intent in early Human–AI systems is explicit intent.

Examples include:

  • button press;
  • typed command;
  • spoken command;
  • touch selection;
  • joystick input;
  • gesture;
  • confirmed gaze selection.

Represent explicit intent as:

IE(t)

Explicit intent has two major advantages.

First, it is directly observable.

Second, it can provide ground truth for training and validating more advanced inference systems.

If the user says:

"Open door,"

then:

IE=Open Door

The machine does not need to guess.

5.3 Intent as a Vector

Complex systems often require more than a single command label.

Define an Intent Vector:

I(t) = [ G, T, D, P, C, U ]

where:

  • G = goal;
  • T = target;
  • D = direction or desired state transition;
  • P = priority;
  • C = confidence;
  • U = uncertainty.

For transportation:

I = [ Navigate, Waypoint B, East/Northeast trajectory, High, 0.96, 0.04 ]

For Hearthstone:

I = [ Reduce stimulation, Room environment, Lower intensity, Moderate, 1.00, 0 ]

The intent representation should therefore preserve both what is wanted and how confidently the system knows it.

5.4 Declared Intent Versus Inferred Intent

The architecture distinguishes:

IE
  • explicit or declared intent,

from:

Î

machine-inferred intent.

This distinction must remain visible throughout the control stack.

For example:

Î1=Reduce screen brightness

may be inferred from:

  • gaze behavior;
  • pupil response;
  • repeated squinting;
  • previous behavior;
  • environmental light level.

That does not mean the person necessarily wants the screen dimmed.

Therefore, the system should represent:

P(Ik|H,E,B)

rather than claiming:

Ik=known

where:

  • H is human state;
  • E is environment;
  • B is behavioral history.

5.5 The Intent Probability Distribution

Rather than selecting one intention too early, the system should preserve a probability distribution:

P(I) = [ P(I1), P(I2), ..., P(In) ]

For example:

P(Turn Left)=0.71
P(Continue Straight)=0.18
P(Slow Down)=0.11

This representation is safer than immediately converting the strongest estimate into a machine command.

The system should also know how concentrated the distribution is.

If:

P(I1)=0.35
P(I2)=0.34
P(I3)=0.31

the machine should interpret that as:

intent unresolved.

Not:

execute I1.

5.6 Confidence Thresholds

For a given action Ak, define an intent-confidence threshold:

θI,k

The system may permit automatic execution only if:

P(Ik)≥θI,k

The threshold should depend upon consequence.

For low-risk actions:

θI,k

may be relatively modest.

For high-risk actions:

θI,k→ 1

conceptually.

Changing room music is not equivalent to changing a vehicle trajectory.

Therefore:

Required certainty must scale with consequence.

5.7 Confirmation as an Information Channel

When intent remains uncertain, the system should ask.

This sounds obvious, but it is an important architecture feature.

If:

UI>θU

the machine may transition to:

Confirm

rather than:

Execute

For example:

"Did you want me to lower the lights?"

or:

"Confirm destination change."

This creates a hybrid interface:

Inference + Human Confirmation

which may provide most of the convenience of intent-aware technology without requiring dangerous assumptions.

5.8 Negative Intent and Veto

A human system must recognize that stop is not just another command.

It is a sovereignty signal.

Define:

Iveto

A validated explicit veto should have extremely high authority:

Iveto > Îmachine

The machine should never say:

"I inferred that you actually wanted to continue."

The architecture therefore distinguishes:

Goal Intent

from:

Veto Intent

and gives veto a privileged safety role.

5.9 Temporal Persistence of Intent

Human intent can change rapidly.

A single instantaneous signal may therefore be insufficient.

Define:

I(t)

and evaluate persistence over:

[t-T,t]

A stable intended action may require:

P(Ik|τ)≥θI

for:

τ≥τmin

This prevents transient noise, fleeting attention, or involuntary physiological changes from being interpreted as commands.

For low-risk systems, τmin may be short.

For high-risk systems, additional persistence or confirmation may be required.

5.10 Intent Initiation and Intent Cancellation

Any control system using inferred intent should explicitly model both the beginning and end of an intention.

Define:

IkON

and:

IkOFF

A system that recognizes only initiation may continue acting after the human has changed their mind.

Therefore:

Ik(t) = { 1, intent active ; 0, intent inactive }

must be updated continuously.

The machine should never treat intent as permanently latched unless the action itself requires persistence.

5.11 Target Identification

Intent often requires knowing what object the person means.

Suppose the user looks toward three controls and says:

"Open that."

The machine must infer both:

I=Open

and:

T=Target

The full command becomes:

I = (I,T)

Target identification may use:

  • gaze;
  • pointing;
  • context;
  • prior interaction;
  • explicit labels;
  • spatial mapping.

Intent without target resolution should not trigger action.

5.12 Gaze-Assisted Intent

Gaze is especially useful because it can narrow candidate targets.

Define:

G(t)

as gaze direction.

Then:

P(Tj|G,E)

can estimate which target the user is attending to.

Intent estimation then becomes:

P(Ik,Tj|H,G,E,C)

This is substantially more robust than attempting to infer full intent from physiology alone.

In a future cockpit, gaze may help distinguish:

observing an object

from:

intending to act upon it.

Those are not the same state.

5.13 Gesture-Assisted Intent

Gestures can similarly provide directional information.

Examples include:

  • pointing;
  • hand selection;
  • head movement;
  • posture shift;
  • deliberate physical signal.

A gesture vector may be represented:

Gbody = [ position, velocity, orientation, confidence ]

Combined with context:

P(I|Gbody,E)

may become highly reliable.

Human–AI Coherence Systems therefore does not assume the future interface eliminates movement.

Rather, it creates a hierarchy in which multiple channels cooperate.

5.14 Voice and Language Intent

Statistical AI is particularly powerful in extracting intent from language.

A spoken command:

"Take me home, but avoid the highway."

contains:

  • destination;
  • route preference;
  • implicit navigation objective.

Represent:

Ilanguage = L(text,context)

where L is a language interpretation function.

This is one area where conventional Statistical AI can remain extremely useful within the larger Human–AI Coherence architecture.

Field AI does not need to replace language models.

The four-engine architecture can distribute tasks according to substrate strengths.

5.15 Neural Intent

Some brain–computer interfaces already infer limited categories of user intention from neural signals under controlled conditions.

Represent neural features:

N(t)

and a decoder:

ÎN = DN(N)

The decoder may identify:

  • left/right motor imagery;
  • target selection;
  • attention toward a stimulus;
  • binary or multi-class choices.

The critical limitation remains:

ÎN is task-specific inference, not general mind reading.

The machine only knows what experimental mapping has been validated.

5.16 Physiological Intent Is Even More Indirect

Cardiac, respiratory, autonomic, and behavioral state may correlate with decision processes.

They do not generally identify a specific intended command on their own.

Therefore:

P(I|H)

should initially be treated as weak unless supported by task context or other channels.

For example, elevated arousal does not tell the system whether the person wants to:

  • stop;
  • accelerate;
  • leave;
  • continue;
  • speak;
  • remain still.

State can influence confidence in intent inference.

It should not automatically become the command itself.

5.17 Contextual Intent

Context dramatically narrows the interpretation problem.

Suppose a pilot is approaching a waypoint.

Candidate intentions may be:

{ Turn, Hold, Descend, Stop }

rather than every possible human intention.

Therefore:

P(I|H,C)

may be much more informative than:

P(I|H)

where C represents task context.

A safe system should therefore infer intent only within a bounded action space.

5.18 Action Vocabulary

Every Human–AI system should define the set of actions it is allowed to interpret:

A = { A1,A2,...,An }

For Hearthstone:

AHS = { LightUp, LightDown, SoundUp, SoundDown, VibrationOn, VibrationOff }

For transportation:

AT = { Accelerate, Decelerate, Turn, Hold, Stop, Navigate }

The machine should not invent actions outside its authorized set.

This creates a finite control grammar.

5.19 Intent Grammar

More complex actions can be constructed compositionally.

For example:

I= Verb + Target + Magnitude + Constraint

So:

I= Navigate + Waypoint B + Normal speed + Avoid Zone C

A formal intent packet may therefore include:

PI = { Action, Target, Magnitude, Duration, Priority, Constraints, Confidence }

This becomes valuable for interoperability among multiple Christos systems.

5.20 The Human–AI Intent Bridge

The architecture can now define an Intent Bridge:

Human
↓
Explicit Input + Gaze + Gesture + Voice + Neural Signal + Physiology + Context
↓
Intent Estimator
↓
P(Ik),UI
↓
Confirmation / Safety Gate
↓
Command

This is the practical Human–AI Coherence Bridge before any direct field-coupling hypothesis is introduced.

5.21 Intent and the Coherence State Vector

Intent should be interpreted in relation to the current human state.

Therefore:

P(Ik) = P( Ik | H, E, C )

However, coherence must not automatically dominate intent.

A person outside a preferred physiological envelope may still make a legitimate decision.

For example:

CH<θC

does not imply:

I=invalid.

Instead, lower state confidence may modify how much control authority is granted to inferred intent.

Explicit commands remain separate.

5.22 Coherence-Gated Intent Authority

Define:

αI

as the authority assigned to inferred intent.

A conceptual function is:

αI = F( ConfI, Q, U, CH, Risk )

High confidence, high signal quality, low uncertainty, and low risk may permit:

αI↑.

Low confidence or increased risk produces:

αI↓.

This creates a continuum:

Observe → Suggest → Assist → Execute

instead of a binary choice.

5.23 False Positive Intent

The most dangerous error in direct-control systems is often not failure to detect intent.

It is detecting intent that does not exist.

Define:

FP= P( Î=1 | I=0 )

For low-risk applications, some false positives may merely be inconvenient.

For transportation, they may be unacceptable.

Therefore, the optimization objective should not simply maximize accuracy.

Instead:

L = λFPFP + λFNFN

where:

λFP

may become very large for safety-critical actions.

5.24 No-Command State

The system must explicitly model:

I0=No Command

This is essential.

If the classifier is forced to choose among:

{Left,Right,Forward,Stop}

even when the user intends nothing, it will generate false commands.

The intent space should therefore be:

I = { I0, I1, I2,...,In }

where I0 may be the default state.

5.25 Intent Hold

In continuous control, there must also be a deliberate hold state.

For example:

IH=Maintain Current State

Without this, the system may continuously search for changes.

In transportation:

IH

can mean:

maintain current trajectory.

In Hearthstone:

maintain current environmental configuration.

In an AI interface:

continue current interaction state.

This reduces unnecessary oscillation.

5.26 Intent Conflict

Humans may generate contradictory signals.

Speech says:

continue.

Gesture says:

stop.

Gaze shifts away.

Physiology changes abruptly.

The machine should not silently decide which one is “real.”

Define a conflict measure:

ΓI = Conflict( IE, IG, IN, IH )

If:

ΓI>θΓ

the system should transition to:

Clarify

or:

Safe Hold.

5.27 Multi-Step Intent

Some intentions are hierarchical.

For example:

I1=Travel to Indianapolis

contains many lower-level actions:

I2=Select Route
I3=Control Speed
I4=Avoid Obstacles

The human need not directly control every sub-action.

This introduces hierarchical intent:

Ihigh → { Ilow,1, Ilow,2,... }

AI can therefore translate high-level human purpose into lower-level machine actions.

This is one of the most important distinctions between human sovereignty and manual micromanagement.

The person provides the objective.

The machine may execute the detailed control process within authorized constraints.

5.28 Human Purpose, Machine Execution

This can be written:

GH → Planner → A1,A2,...,An

where GH is the human goal.

The machine does not determine the ultimate objective.

It decomposes the objective.

This produces a core design principle:

Human defines purpose. AI manages complexity.

That principle scales from home automation to navigation.

5.29 Statistical AI and Intent

Within the four-engine architecture, Statistical AI is well suited to:

  • language interpretation;
  • contextual prediction;
  • behavior pattern recognition;
  • semantic intent classification;
  • planning;
  • probabilistic inference.

Therefore:

Isemantic

may be largely processed through Statistical AI.

This does not make Statistical AI the entire control architecture.

It becomes one engine within a larger system.

5.30 Field AI and Intent

Field AI introduces a different possibility.

Instead of representing intent only symbolically, a human-state or intent vector may be translated into a resonant state.

Define:

TIF: I → F

such that:

I → Ftarget

The Field AI network may then evolve toward an attractor associated with that intent class or system configuration.

This could potentially provide:

  • continuous-state control;
  • pattern completion;
  • noise tolerance;
  • physical attractor memory;
  • analog state interpolation.

These are architectural hypotheses requiring prototype validation.

5.31 Intent as an Attractor

Suppose each validated intent corresponds to an attractor:

Ak

Then:

F(t)→Ak

could represent machine recognition of intent Ik.

Rather than:

binary class=3

the system may physically settle into a resonant pattern corresponding to:

I3.

This is conceptually compatible with the broader Field AI architecture.

Whether it provides an advantage over conventional classifiers must be tested.

5.32 Intent Translation Layer

This suggests a general translation architecture:

H + I
↓
Intent Translation Layer
↓
Statistical Representation + Field Representation + Machine Command Representation

The same human intention can therefore exist in multiple computational forms.

This becomes important later when the four-engine architecture is integrated.

5.33 Bidirectional Intent

A truly adaptive machine must also communicate its own intended action to the user.

Define:

IM

machine action intention.

Before execution, the system may expose:

IM=I am about to reduce lighting by 20%

or:

IM=I am initiating autonomous stabilization

This creates mutual legibility.

The human knows what the machine is about to do.

The machine knows what it believes the human wants.

This is far safer than a hidden inference system.

5.34 Predictive Preview

For higher-risk actions, the system can show or simulate the predicted outcome before executing.

Let:

Ŝt+1 = Model( St,Ak )

The user can inspect:

If this action is executed, here is the predicted result.

This may be visual, auditory, haptic, or informational.

Predictive preview provides another safeguard between intent and action.

5.35 Intent Logging

Every high-consequence action should preserve a traceable record:

LI = { timestamp, inputs, intent estimate, confidence, confirmation, action }

This allows later analysis of:

  • false commands;
  • missed commands;
  • conflicts;
  • operator overrides;
  • model failure.

It also allows validation of the system over time.

5.36 Intent Replay

Experimental systems should support replay.

Researchers can reconstruct:

Ht
It
Mt
At

and ask:

Why did the system act?

This is essential for debugging safety-critical human–AI coupling.

5.37 From Input Device to Intent Device

The evolution of interface architecture can now be represented:

Stage 0

Human → Button → Machine

Stage 1

Human → Voice/Gesture → Machine

Stage 2

Human → Multimodal Intent Estimator → Machine

Stage 3

Human State + Intent → Adaptive AI → Machine

Stage 4

Human ⇄ AI ⇄ Physical System

Stage 5

Proposed:

Human Intent → Resonant/Field Interface → System

The progression is evolutionary rather than discontinuous.

5.38 The Phase Key Reinterpreted as an Interface Architecture

Within the broader Christos transportation and Sovereign Explorer Vessel architecture, the Phase Key has been described as a proposed biofield-coupled intention transmitter.

Human–AI Coherence Systems provides a more structured pathway toward that concept.

Rather than beginning with:

Intent → Field

the developmental sequence becomes:

Explicit Intent
↓

↓

The Phase Key therefore becomes not merely an object, but the frontier endpoint of a broader intent-translation architecture.

5.39 Conservative Phase Key Prototype

A conservative prototype could operate entirely through known mechanisms.

For example:

HRV + Respiration + Touch + Voice + Motion

feed:

Intent Estimator

which drives:

Resonant Output

through:

  • audio;

  • optical signals;
  • electromagnetic actuation within safe limits.

The crystal or resonant structure can function as an experimental physical component without assuming it directly reads intention.

This provides an incremental build path.

5.40 The Frontier Direct-Intent Hypothesis

The stronger Christos hypothesis is that human intention may eventually produce a measurable effect through an additional resonant or field-level coupling channel.

Represent this hypothetical pathway as:

IH → BH → CHM

where:

  • IH = human intention;
  • BH = proposed biological field state;
  • CHM = measurable human–machine coupling.

This pathway remains unvalidated.

To support it, experiments would need to demonstrate:

Effectintent ≠ Effectcontrol

after controlling known pathways.

5.41 Testing Direct Intent

A rigorous experiment might include:

Condition A

Explicit physical command.

Condition B

Intent without physical command.

Condition C

Sham intent period.

Condition D

No participant.

Condition E

Participant present but performing unrelated mental task.

Sensors and system outputs should be blinded where possible.

The question becomes:

Does the machine exhibit a reproducible state transition associated specifically with the preregistered intent condition?

If not, the direct-intent hypothesis is not supported.

5.42 Preventing Ideomotor Confounds

Intent experiments must control involuntary physical movement.

The ideomotor effect demonstrates that intention can produce subtle muscular actions without conscious awareness.

Therefore, experiments should monitor:

  • EMG;
  • motion;
  • pressure;
  • touch;
  • posture;
  • respiration;
  • gaze.

If the machine response can be explained by micro-movement, the experiment has not demonstrated direct field coupling.

This is especially important in crystal or hand-held Phase Key experiments.

5.43 Electromagnetic Confounds

The human body also produces measurable electrical and magnetic activity.

Any experimental resonant interface should therefore characterize known electromagnetic coupling.

If:

Emeasured

can be explained by conventional bioelectric or electromagnetic signals, then a new mechanism is unnecessary.

Only residual effects beyond adequately controlled known mechanisms would justify further investigation.

5.44 Intent Strength

The architecture should not assume that subjective intensity corresponds linearly to machine effect.

Nevertheless, experimental intent strength can be parameterized.

For example:

Is∈{0,1,2,3}

representing preregistered levels such as:

  • no intent;
  • weak intentional focus;
  • moderate focus;
  • strong focus.

Researchers can test whether:

Response ∝ Is

or whether no relationship exists.

This provides a dose-response style test of the hypothesis.

5.45 Intent Directionality

A stronger experiment would test opposing intentions.

For example:

I+=Increase
I-=Decrease

If the system responds:

Δ X+>0

and:

Δ X-<0

under blinded replicated conditions, that would be stronger evidence than merely observing a nonspecific difference between intent and no-intent periods.

Directionality matters.

5.46 Intent Specificity

Even stronger evidence would require multiple distinct target states.

Suppose:

I1→ S1
I2→ S2
I3→ S3

If a system can reliably discriminate among them without conventional input, the hypothesis becomes significantly more interesting.

The experimental standard should therefore progress from:

detection

to:

direction

to:

specificity.

5.47 Intent Bandwidth

Any direct-control system also has an information-rate question.

If one can classify N reliable intent states at rate r, then a rough command bandwidth may be represented:

BI ≈ rlog2N

bits per unit time.

This allows comparison against:

  • keyboard;
  • speech;
  • gesture;
  • conventional BCI;
  • direct-intent experimental interfaces.

A frontier interface does not become useful merely because an effect exists.

It must eventually support adequate information transfer.

5.48 Accuracy Is Not Enough

A direct-intent system might report:

Accuracy=90%

which sounds impressive.

Yet if the remaining 10% produces uncontrolled movement, the system may be unusable.

Evaluation must therefore include:

  • false-positive rate;
  • false-negative rate;
  • latency;
  • command persistence;
  • cancellation reliability;
  • confusion matrix;
  • information transfer rate;
  • safety response.

This is especially critical for transportation.

5.49 The Transportation Progression

The intent architecture allows the Christos transportation concept to be developed through stages.

Stage 1: Conventional Controls

Steering, pedals, displays, voice.

Stage 2: Intent Observation

The system predicts what the pilot is likely to do but does not act.

Stage 3: Intent Assistance

The system prepares likely commands.

Stage 4: Coherence-Gated Assistance

Stage 5: Intent-Primary Control

Validated multimodal intent becomes a primary input.

Stage 6: Resonant Intent Translation

Field AI or resonant states represent pilot intent.

Stage 7: Direct Coupling

Frontier hypothesis: direct intention contributes measurable control information without conventional physical input.

This creates a legitimate research pathway from existing human–machine systems toward the much more ambitious architecture portrayed in the transportation papers.

The Sovereign Explorer Vessel represents the most advanced application of this progression.
