This prevents:

DATA COLLECTED FOR SAFETY

from silently becoming:

DATA USED FOR SURVEILLANCE.

19.34 Context Collapse

The same biological measurement can have radically different implications in different contexts.

A heart-rate signal collected during a personal wellness session is not automatically appropriate for:

Employment evaluation.

Insurance decisions.

Credit decisions.

Advertising.

Political profiling.

Legal judgment.

Access control.

The architecture should resist such context collapse.

19.35 No Coherence Score as Social Rank

One of the clearest boundaries in this entire paper is:

A COHERENCE SCORE MUST NOT BECOME A HUMAN RANKING SYSTEM.

A measured or estimated coherence state describes a context-dependent system variable.

It is not a measure of:

Intelligence.

Moral worth.

Spiritual worth.

Social value.

Trustworthiness.

Employment value.

Citizenship value.

Human worth.

19.36 State Is Not Identity

A person may move through:

High coherence.

Low coherence.

Stress.

Fatigue.

Recovery.

Focus.

Distraction.

These are states.

They are not permanent identities.

Therefore:

STATE != IDENTITY.

19.37 No Coherence Caste System

The architecture explicitly rejects any future system in which access to:

Employment.

Education.

Transportation.

Housing.

Financial services.

Healthcare.

Civic participation.

or fundamental rights

is determined by a generalized coherence ranking.

That would transform a human-assistance architecture into a social-control architecture.

19.38 The System Must Not Reward Performative Physiology

If people know that a physiological metric controls access or status, they may begin optimizing for the metric rather than the underlying objective.

This can corrupt both measurement and behavior.

The purpose of coherence estimation is functional adaptation, not social scoring.

19.39 Human-State Data Must Not Become a Loyalty Test

Physiological responses cannot legitimately establish ideological loyalty.

A person's bodily response to:

A statement.

A symbol.

A person.

An institution.

A political idea.

A religious idea.

does not provide a valid basis for determining allegiance or moral standing.

19.40 No Automated Truth Machine

The architecture must reject the idea that multimodal biological sensing automatically creates a perfect lie detector.

Physiological arousal is not equivalent to deception.

Therefore:

AROUSAL != DECEPTION.
COHERENCE != HONESTY.
STRESS != GUILT.

19.41 Frontier Sensing Requires Stronger Boundaries

If future experiments ever demonstrate reliable sensing beyond conventional physiological channels, privacy protections must become stronger, not weaker.

Increasing sensing capability should increase governance requirements.

19.42 The Frontier Privacy Rule

Suppose a future system claims to measure some proposed field variable associated with human state.

Until validated, that variable remains experimental.

If eventually validated, the existence of the capability would not establish unrestricted permission to use it.

Therefore:

DISCOVERY OF A NEW HUMAN SIGNAL DOES NOT CREATE OWNERSHIP OF THAT SIGNAL.

19.43 The Phase Key Problem

The Phase Key architecture proposes increasingly intimate coupling among:

Human state.

Intent.

System configuration.

Navigation.

Physical response.

If such systems are ever experimentally realized, they create a profound sovereignty requirement.

The machine must distinguish:

WHAT THE HUMAN EXPERIENCES

from:

WHAT THE HUMAN INTENDS TO COMMAND.

19.44 Experience Is Not Command

A fleeting:

Thought.

Emotion.

Image.

Fear.

Impulse.

Physiological reaction.

must not automatically become machine action.

Therefore:

MENTAL CONTENT != COMMAND.

19.45 Intention Requires Commitment

A useful future interface may distinguish between:

PRE-INTENT.
CONSIDERED INTENT.
ACTIONABLE INTENT.
CONFIRMED COMMAND.

The exact classification requires research.

The principle is that machines should not execute every detectable fluctuation of the human interior.

19.46 The Thought-to-Action Firewall

For high-consequence systems, the architecture should maintain:

PRIVATE HUMAN STATE

->

POSSIBLE INTENT

->

INTERPRETED INTENT

->

CONFIRMED INTENT

->

AUTHORIZED COMMAND.

This creates a firewall between inner experience and physical execution.

19.47 The Right to Think Without Acting

Humans imagine actions they never intend to perform.

Humans simulate possibilities internally.

Humans experience intrusive thoughts.

Humans change their minds.

A consciousness-integrated control architecture must therefore preserve:

THE RIGHT TO THINK WITHOUT THE MACHINE ACTING.

19.48 The Right to Remain Uninterpreted

Not every biological fluctuation requires explanation.

Not every silence requires inference.

Not every hesitation requires classification.

Not every emotion needs to become a data object.

Where functionality does not require interpretation, the system should be capable of leaving the human uninterpreted.

19.49 Privacy Mode

A Human–AI Coherence System should support clearly defined privacy states where practical.

For example:

FULL ASSISTANCE.
LIMITED SENSING.
SAFETY-ONLY SENSING.
MANUAL INTERACTION.
PRIVATE MODE.

The available modes depend on the application.

19.50 Safety-Only Mode

A particularly important configuration may preserve only measurements necessary for immediate physical safety while disabling optional adaptive inference.

This allows the system to remain protective without continuously modeling the person.

19.51 Data Separation

Different categories of human data should be logically separated where appropriate:

IDENTITY DATA.
BIOLOGICAL DATA.
BEHAVIORAL DATA.
INTENT DATA.
AUTHORIZATION DATA.
MEDICAL DATA.
RESEARCH DATA.
SYSTEM TELEMETRY.

Combining them should require explicit justification.

19.52 Identity Need Not Follow Every Signal

A system may sometimes need physiological state without needing permanent identity linkage.

Research and development should therefore consider:

Pseudonymization.

De-identification where genuinely effective.

Short-lived identifiers.

Session-specific processing.

Aggregate analysis.

The correct method depends on the threat model and use case.

19.53 Re-Identification Risk

Removing a person's name does not necessarily make biological data anonymous.

Unique signal patterns and combinations of metadata may permit re-identification.

Therefore:

NAME REMOVAL != GUARANTEED ANONYMITY.

19.54 Retention Has Consequences

The longer intimate data exists, the longer it can potentially be:

Breached.

Misused.

Reinterpreted.

Combined with future datasets.

Used for purposes never anticipated when collected.

Retention should therefore be intentional.

19.55 Retention Classes

Data may be categorized as:

EPHEMERAL.
SESSION-LIMITED.
SHORT-TERM OPERATIONAL.
RESEARCH RETENTION.
REGULATORY RETENTION.
USER-REQUESTED ARCHIVE.

Each class should have defined rules.

19.56 Delete Means More Than Hide

Where deletion is promised and technically applicable, removing a user interface reference while retaining unrestricted copies elsewhere does not satisfy the spirit of deletion.

System design should identify:

Primary copies.

Caches.

Backups.

Derived datasets.

Model-training implications.

Audit requirements.

Legal retention requirements.

The user should not be promised deletion that the architecture cannot actually perform.

19.57 Model Training Requires Separate Attention

Human biological and cognitive-adjacent data should not automatically become training material for future models simply because it passed through the system.

Operational processing and model training are separate purposes.

Therefore:

USE FOR SERVICE != CONSENT TO TRAINING.

19.58 Federated or Local Learning

Where appropriate, future architectures may investigate methods that allow adaptation without centralizing all raw human data.

Possible approaches include:

Local learning.

Federated learning.

Privacy-preserving aggregation.

Secure computation.

Differential privacy for appropriate statistical applications.

These methods do not eliminate privacy risk, but they may reduce unnecessary data concentration.

19.59 The Personal Model

A mature Human–AI Coherence System may eventually maintain a personalized model:

MH.

This could improve:

State estimation.

Interface adaptation.

Intent interpretation.

Safety.

Accessibility.

Personalization.

Such a model may become extremely sensitive.

19.60 The Personal Model Should Serve the Person

The architecture establishes:

MH → benefit of H

as the default design orientation.

A personal model should not quietly become a mechanism for third parties to manipulate the person more effectively.

19.61 Manipulation Is Different From Assistance

Adaptive interfaces naturally influence behavior.

The ethical question is not whether influence exists.

It is whether the influence serves transparent human objectives or covert external objectives.

19.62 Coherence Optimization Can Become Manipulation

Suppose the AI learns that certain:

Sounds.

Colors.

Phrases.

Rhythms.

Environmental settings.

Feedback patterns.

alter measured human state.

That knowledge could be used to support regulation.

It could also be used to manipulate behavior.

The technical capability is similar.

The governance objective is not.

19.63 No Covert Entrainment

The architecture should therefore prohibit covert attempts to alter human state through adaptive stimuli without appropriate authorization.

This is particularly important for proposed:

Acoustic entrainment.

Visual entrainment.

Respiratory entrainment.

Field-based entrainment.

Neural stimulation.

Other physiological modulation.

19.64 Therapeutic Context Requires Its Own Standards

A person voluntarily using a clinically appropriate intervention is different from a consumer system secretly attempting to modify physiology.

Medical and therapeutic applications require:

Evidence.

Consent.

Professional standards where applicable.

Regulatory compliance.

Adverse-event monitoring.

Appropriate clinical oversight.

19.65 The AI Must Not Create Dependency as an Objective

A system optimized for engagement may discover that dependence increases usage.

A Human–AI Coherence System should not deliberately optimize toward making the human less capable of functioning without it.

The objective should instead include preservation or enhancement of human capability.

19.66 Assistance Should Preserve Agency

Where possible, successful assistance should help the person become:

Better informed.

More capable.

More aware.

More effective.

More able to make deliberate choices.

The system should not require learned helplessness to justify its existence.

19.67 The Human Can Disagree With the AI

The system should permit:

“I disagree.”

“Show me why.”

“Give me another option.”

“Do not do that.”

“Stop adapting to me.”

“Use manual mode.”

“Forget this session where applicable.”

Human disagreement is not a system error.

19.68 Explanation Supports Sovereignty

When AI recommendations materially affect the human, the system should provide useful explanations appropriate to the context.

Not every mathematical operation needs to be exposed.

The human should understand enough to make a meaningful decision.

19.69 Recommendation Strength Should Be Visible

The interface should distinguish:

OPTION.
SUGGESTION.
STRONG RECOMMENDATION.
SAFETY WARNING.
MANDATORY SAFETY INTERVENTION.

Without this distinction, assistance can masquerade as authority.

19.70 The System Must Reveal When It Is Inferring

If the system knows something because the human explicitly said it, that is different from inferring it from physiology or behavior.

Where consequential, the interface should distinguish:

YOU TOLD ME THIS

from:

I INFERRED THIS.

19.71 Inference Confidence Must Remain Visible

A useful representation is:

ÎH = Ij, qI = 0.63

rather than presenting:

THE HUMAN INTENDS Ij

as certain fact.

Confidence should travel with the inference.

19.72 Multi-Human Privacy

Section 17 introduced multi-human coherence.

That creates another challenge.

One participant's data may reveal information about another.

For example:

Communication patterns.

Shared location.

Interaction timing.

Group physiological synchrony.

Team-performance measurements.

Group privacy therefore cannot always be reduced to individual privacy.

19.73 Shared Systems Need Information Boundaries

A pilot may need to know:

PASSENGER MEDICAL EMERGENCY DETECTED.

The pilot may not need the passenger's entire biological history.

A research lead may need:

PARTICIPANT WITHDRAWN.

They may not need private reasons for withdrawal.

Therefore access should follow operational need.

19.74 Role-Based Data Access

Extend the Section 17 authority matrix into information access.

Define:

P(i,d)

where:

i = participant or system role.

d = data class.

P(i,d) defines permitted access.

Control authority and information authority should not be assumed identical.

19.75 The AI Also Has Permissions

AI components should not automatically receive unrestricted access to every available data source.

Different engines may receive only the information required for their function.

A navigation engine may not need medical history.

A biomedical controller may not need private communications.

A statistical assistant may not need raw neural data.

19.76 Four-Engine Data Boundaries

The Four-Engine architecture therefore requires explicit information routing.

Statistical AI.

Field AI.

Quantum AI.

Photon AI.

should not be treated as one undifferentiated intelligence with universal access.

Each engine should receive only justified inputs.

19.77 Cross-Engine Fusion Is a Privacy Event

Combining multiple data streams can reveal information not apparent in any individual stream.

Therefore multimodal fusion itself requires governance.

Conceptually:

D1 + D2 + D3

may produce inferred information:

I*

that none of the original datasets explicitly contained.

19.78 Inference Amplification

This means privacy risk may grow nonlinearly with data integration.

A system possessing:

Gaze.

Voice.

HRV.

Location.

Behavior.

Neural activity.

may infer far more than a system possessing any one signal.

Therefore:

MORE DATA DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY MEAN BETTER ARCHITECTURE.

19.79 Data Concentration Is a Security Problem

The most personalized Human–AI system may also become the most attractive target.

A database containing:

Identity.

Physiology.

Intent patterns.

Behavior.

Location.

Personal models.

Authorization history.

could create severe consequences if compromised.

Privacy architecture therefore directly becomes security architecture.

19.80 Privacy by Architecture

The strongest privacy control is often not a policy promising that sensitive data will never be misused.

It is an architecture that never unnecessarily possesses the data in the first place.

Therefore:

DO NOT PROTECT WHAT YOU DO NOT NEED TO COLLECT.

19.81 Sovereignty by Architecture

Likewise, human sovereignty should not depend solely on a company promising to behave well.

It should be encoded into:

Permissions.

Local processing.

Data separation.

Consent mechanisms.

Hardware controls.

Audit systems.

Revocation pathways.

Authority boundaries.

19.82 Ownership Versus Stewardship

Legal ownership models differ across jurisdictions and data classes.

This paper therefore does not attempt to declare a universal legal property doctrine for biological information.

Its engineering principle is simpler:

THE SYSTEM SHOULD TREAT INTIMATE HUMAN DATA AS SOMETHING ENTRUSTED TO IT, NOT SOMETHING IT HAS CAPTURED.

19.83 Research Participants

Research creates additional obligations.

Experimental human-state systems should clearly distinguish:

Research participation.

Ordinary product use.

Clinical use.

Operational use.

Participation in research should follow appropriate ethical review and informed-consent requirements.

19.84 Experimental Data Must Be Labeled Experimental

If a proposed coherence variable has not been clinically or scientifically validated, the system must not present it to the participant as established medical fact.

For example:

EXPERIMENTAL COHERENCE ESTIMATE

is different from:

MEDICAL DIAGNOSIS.

19.85 No Diagnostic Inflation

A research metric should not quietly become:

A diagnosis.

A prognosis.

A treatment recommendation.

A psychological label.

A fitness determination.

without the evidence and regulatory pathway required for that use.

19.86 The BFI Boundary

The proposed BFI Patch and related frontier sensing architectures require exactly this discipline.

Conventional measurable channels should remain distinguishable from proposed Christfield Gradient measurements.

If a variable such as:

X

is operationally defined for experimentation, the interface must not imply that X represents an established biological field until evidence supports that conclusion.

19.87 Experimental Variable, Not Human Essence

Even if X eventually demonstrates repeatable relationships with physiology or behavior:

X ≠ human essence.

No instrument should claim to measure the totality of a person.

19.88 The Harmonic Kodex Boundary

Higher-tier speculative layers of the architecture must receive the strongest epistemic separation.

A proposed mapping between:

Human state.

Coherence.

Intention.

Field interaction.

Harmonic structure.

may be investigated experimentally.

It must not become an unquestionable classification system imposed on people.

19.89 Spiritual Interpretation Must Remain Voluntary

Where users personally interpret coherence through:

Spiritual.

Philosophical.

Religious.

Contemplative.

  • or metaphysical frameworks,
  • the system may support their chosen context where appropriate.

It should not impose one metaphysical interpretation as a technical fact.

19.90 No Machine Authority Over Human Meaning

An AI can help a person explore meaning.

It cannot possess final authority over:

Who the person is.

What their life means.

What they should believe.

What their spiritual state is.

What their ultimate purpose is.

These questions exceed the legitimate authority of the machine.

19.91 Human Purpose Remains Upstream

This returns to one of the central principles of the paper:

HUMAN PURPOSE > MACHINE PROCEDURE.

The machine may improve procedure.

It does not inherit ownership of purpose.

19.92 Sovereignty Under High Automation

The more capable the system becomes, the easier it becomes for humans to stop understanding what it is doing.

High automation therefore requires mechanisms for:

Inspection.

Interruption.

Mode selection.

Explanation.

Authority review.

Fallback.

19.93 Convenience Cannot Quietly Erase Control

Users may voluntarily delegate routine decisions.

Delegation can be useful.

The architecture must distinguish:

DELEGATION

from:

PERMANENT SURRENDER OF AUTHORITY.

19.94 Delegation Is Scoped

A human may authorize:

“Manage cabin temperature automatically.”

That does not authorize:

“Modify every environmental variable affecting my physiology.”

Delegation should be bounded by:

Function.

Duration.

Context.

Consequence.

19.95 Delegation Is Revocable

Where safety permits:

AH→ AI(t)

should be retractable.

The human can reclaim delegated authority.

19.96 No Dark Patterns for Sovereignty

The system should not make privacy or autonomy technically available but practically impossible to exercise.

Examples include:

Needlessly complicated opt-outs.

Repeated pressure to re-enable sensing.

Degraded unrelated functionality.

Misleading interface language.

Hidden defaults.

Human sovereignty should be usable.

19.97 The Right to Disconnect

Where physical safety and application requirements permit, a person should be able to leave the coherence loop.

This may mean:

Removing a wearable.

Disabling optional sensing.

Ending a session.

Switching to manual interaction.

Disconnecting personal data.

Leaving the system entirely.

19.98 Disconnect Must Have a Defined System Response

If a human disappears from the sensing loop:

H(t) → UNAVAILABLE,

the system should know what to do.

Depending on the application:

Continue conventional operation.

Reduce automation.

Transfer control.

Enter restricted mode.

Request another authorized operator.

Move toward safe state.

The machine must not fabricate continued human authorization.

19.99 Absence Is Not Consent

If the human stops responding:

NO RESPONSE

does not automatically mean:

YES.

This becomes particularly important in:

Medical systems.

Experimental systems.

Financially consequential actions.

High-risk physical systems.

Data-sharing decisions.

19.100 Human Sovereignty Principle

The Human–AI Coherence System ultimately requires a boundary stronger than ordinary interface design.

As sensing becomes more intimate, intelligence becomes more adaptive, and control becomes more physically capable, the human must not disappear inside the architecture.

The governing principles are:

THE MODEL OF THE HUMAN IS NOT THE HUMAN.
MEASUREMENT DOES NOT CREATE OWNERSHIP.
INFERENCE DOES NOT CREATE TRUTH.
MENTAL CONTENT DOES NOT CREATE COMMAND.
ASSISTANCE DOES NOT CREATE AUTHORITY.
CONSENT TO ONE PURPOSE DOES NOT CREATE CONSENT TO EVERY PURPOSE.
COHERENCE DOES NOT CREATE HUMAN RANK.
THE HUMAN RETAINS THE RIGHT TO CORRECT, REFUSE, DISAGREE, WITHDRAW, AND WHERE SAFELY POSSIBLE, DISCONNECT.

The purpose of increasingly intimate human-machine coupling is not to dissolve the human into the machine.

It is to create a machine capable of working more naturally with the human without acquiring ownership of the human in the process.

THE CLOSER THE MACHINE COMES TO THE HUMAN INTERIOR, THE STRONGER THE BOUNDARY AROUND HUMAN SOVEREIGNTY MUST BECOME.

Section 20 is where these boundaries become active defenses. We move from who should have access to what happens when someone deliberately tries to obtain access, spoof human intent, corrupt biological sensing, manipulate the AI, compromise an actuator, impersonate an authorized operator, or turn the coherence interface itself into an attack surface.

XXXV. Section 20: Security and Adversarial Conditions

Identity Protection, Sensor Integrity, Intent Authentication, AI Defense, Control Security, and Resilience Under Attack

20.1 Security Begins Where Trust Can Be Exploited

Sections 18 and 19 established two boundaries.

Section 18 asked:

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SOMETHING FAILS?

Section 19 asked:

WHAT IS THE SYSTEM ALLOWED TO KNOW AND DO WITH THE HUMAN?

Security introduces a third question:

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SOMEONE DELIBERATELY TRIES TO MAKE THE SYSTEM DO THE WRONG THING?

Failure can be accidental.

Attack is intentional.

The architecture must survive both.

20.2 The Human–AI Interface Creates a New Attack Surface

A conventional cyberattack may target:

Software.

Credentials.

Networks.

Databases.

Endpoints.

A Human–AI Coherence System potentially adds:

Biological sensors.

Human-state estimators.

Intent interpreters.

Wearables.

Environmental sensors.

AI engines.

Physical actuators.

Proposed field interfaces.

Multi-human authority structures.

The attack surface therefore extends from information systems into the human-machine loop itself.

20.3 The Security Objective

The architecture must protect five things simultaneously:

IDENTITY.
DATA.
INTENT.
AUTHORITY.
PHYSICAL CONTROL.

Compromise of any one can potentially affect the others.

20.4 Identity Is the First Boundary

Before accepting consequential commands, the system must establish:

WHO IS PRESENT?
WHO ISSUED THE COMMAND?
WHAT IDENTITY HAS BEEN AUTHENTICATED?
WHAT ROLE DOES THAT IDENTITY CURRENTLY HOLD?

Authentication should scale with consequence.

20.5 Identity Is Not Authority

A correctly authenticated identity does not automatically possess permission for every function.

Therefore:

IDi ≠ Ai,j

where:

IDi = authenticated identity of human i.

Ai,j = authority of human i over function j.

The system must verify both.

20.6 Authentication Is Not Intent

Even if the system knows exactly who is speaking, it still does not automatically know what they intend.

Therefore:

IDENTITY != INTENT.

This distinction becomes a security boundary.

An attacker may not need to steal identity if they can manipulate intent interpretation.

20.7 The Complete Command Chain

A consequential command should conceptually pass through:

IDENTITY

->

INTENT INTERPRETATION

->

AUTHORITY

->

CONTEXT

->

SAFETY

->

CONTROL TRANSLATION

->

EXECUTION

->

RETURN FLOW.

Security must protect every transition.

20.8 Command Authenticity

The system must distinguish:

A genuine command.

A replayed command.

A fabricated command.

A manipulated command.

An outdated command.

A command issued under invalid authority.

A command generated by another machine pretending to be human.

20.9 Replay Attacks

Suppose an authorized operator previously issued:

OPEN ACCESS PORT.

A recording or captured digital command should not necessarily remain valid indefinitely.

Commands may therefore require:

Fresh authentication.

Session context.

Time validity.

Nonce or challenge mechanisms where appropriate.

Current authority.

Current system state.

20.10 Context Is Part of Command Validity

A valid command in one context may be invalid in another.

For example:

BEGIN EXPERIMENT

may be valid when:

The chamber is empty.

Instrumentation is calibrated.

Containment is active.

Authorization is current.

The same command may become invalid after conditions change.

Therefore:

VALID COMMAND != PERMANENTLY VALID COMMAND.

20.11 Biometric Authentication Has Limits

The architecture may eventually use:

Voice.

Face.

Movement.

Physiological signatures.

Other biometric signals.

Biometrics can improve authentication.

They should not be treated as perfect secrets.

Unlike passwords, biological characteristics may be difficult or impossible to replace.

20.12 Biometrics Should Not Stand Alone for Every Critical Function

High-consequence operations may require multiple independent factors.

Conceptually:

Auth = F(K,P,B,C)

where:

K = something known.

P = something possessed.

B = biometric evidence.

C = contextual validity.

The exact implementation depends on the application.

20.13 Coherence Is Not Authentication

A person displaying a recognized coherence pattern is not necessarily an authorized operator.

Therefore:

COHERENCE != IDENTITY.
COHERENCE != AUTHORITY.

This boundary must remain permanent.

20.14 Physiological Spoofing

If physiological state affects system behavior, an attacker may attempt to manipulate the measured state.

Potential pathways could include:

Sensor interference.

Signal replay.

Synthetic data injection.

Physical manipulation of the sensor.

Environmental interference.

Compromised preprocessing.

The system must therefore treat biological sensing as a security-relevant input.

20.15 Live Signal Verification

Where consequence justifies it, the architecture may need to determine whether incoming physiological data plausibly represents a live, current measurement rather than a replayed stream.

This may involve consistency across:

Time.

Multiple sensors.

Movement.

Physiological relationships.

Environmental context.

No single method should automatically be assumed sufficient.

20.16 Cross-Sensor Consistency

Suppose the system receives:

Heart-rate data.

Respiration.

Movement.

Voice.

If one channel reports a state incompatible with the others, the discrepancy becomes security-relevant.

Conceptually:

ΔS = F(z1,z2,…,zn)

where ΔS represents cross-sensor inconsistency.

Large unexplained inconsistency should reduce trust.

20.17 Anomaly Is Not Proof of Attack

A critical distinction must remain:

ANOMALY != ATTACK.

Sensor failure.

Human physiology.

Environmental disturbance.

Calibration drift.

Software error.

can also produce anomalies.

The architecture should detect suspicious conditions without automatically accusing a person or system.

20.18 Security Confidence

A system may therefore maintain an operational trust estimate:

qS(t)

representing confidence that the relevant sensing, identity, and command pathways remain uncompromised.

This is an engineering state estimate.

It is not proof of security.

20.19 Trust Must Be Continuously Re-Evaluated

Authentication at the beginning of a session does not guarantee integrity forever.

Conditions can change.

Devices can disconnect.

Roles can change.

Networks can be compromised.

Therefore:

qS(t0) ≠ qS(t1)

by assumption.

Trust is temporal.

20.20 Zero Permanent Trust

No subsystem should receive permanent unlimited trust merely because it was trusted once.

This applies to:

Humans.

AI engines.

Sensors.

Software services.

Hardware modules.

Remote systems.

External data.

A better principle is:

VERIFY ACCORDING TO CONSEQUENCE.

20.21 Sensor Integrity Is Foundational

If the system acts on measurements, corrupting those measurements can corrupt control.

An attacker may not need to compromise the AI.

They may only need to alter what the AI believes reality looks like.

Therefore:

CORRUPTED INPUT CAN PRODUCE CORRECTLY EXECUTED WRONG ACTION.

20.22 Sensor Attacks Can Be Physical

Security cannot be limited to software.

Physical sensors may be affected by:

Occlusion.

Vibration.

Electromagnetic interference.

Acoustic interference.

Temperature.

Mechanical displacement.

Optical manipulation.

Electrical injection.

Environmental changes.

The relevant threat depends on the sensor.

20.23 Sensor Fusion Is Not Automatically Secure

Multiple sensors improve robustness only when their failure modes are sufficiently independent.

If every sensor depends on the same compromised processing layer, apparent agreement may be meaningless.

Therefore:

MULTIPLE SIGNALS != MULTIPLE INDEPENDENT WITNESSES.

20.24 Trusted Measurement Path

For safety-critical measurements, the architecture should identify the complete measurement chain:

PHYSICAL PHENOMENON

->

SENSOR

->

SIGNAL CONDITIONING

->

DIGITIZATION

->

PROCESSING

->

STATE ESTIMATION

->

CONTROL DECISION.

Every transition can introduce error or compromise.

20.25 Protect the Return Flow

Attackers may target not only commands but feedback.

If the system performs an action and receives falsified confirmation that the action succeeded, control can diverge from reality.

Therefore return-flow integrity is as important as command integrity.

20.26 False Success Is Dangerous

Suppose the controller commands:

VALVE CLOSED.

The actuator does not close.

A compromised feedback channel reports:

VALVE CLOSED.

The system may proceed under a false state assumption.

This illustrates:

COMMAND SECURITY WITHOUT FEEDBACK SECURITY IS INCOMPLETE.

20.27 Independent Physical Confirmation

For high-consequence operations, important state changes may require independent physical confirmation.

Examples include verifying:

Position.

Pressure.

Temperature.

Electrical isolation.

Mechanical lock.

Containment.

Energy state.

The confirmation method should not depend solely on the same component being verified.

20.28 Intent Injection

A Human–AI Coherence System creates another possible attack class:

INTENT INJECTION.

This means causing the system to interpret an attacker-controlled signal as the authorized human's intent.

Potential pathways could include:

Synthetic voice.

Compromised interface data.

Manipulated sensor input.

Malicious software instructions.

Context poisoning.

The architecture must prevent inferred intent from bypassing authorization.

20.29 Intent Confidence Is Not Security Proof

Even if:

qI = 0.99

the system must still ask:

WHOSE INTENT?
FROM WHAT CHANNEL?
UNDER WHAT AUTHORITY?
IN WHAT CONTEXT?
IS THE CHANNEL TRUSTED?

Therefore:

HIGH INTENT CONFIDENCE != AUTHENTIC COMMAND.

20.30 The Intent Security Gate

Before high-consequence execution, the architecture should conceptually require:

GI = Ivalid ∧ IDvalid ∧ Avalid ∧ Cvalid ∧ Svalid

where:

Ivalid = acceptable intent interpretation.

IDvalid = authenticated identity.

Avalid = current authority.

Cvalid = valid context.

Svalid = safety authorization.

Only then should the command progress toward physical execution.

20.31 Deepfakes and Synthetic Humans

Future systems must assume that:

Voice can be synthesized.

Images can be generated.

Video can be fabricated.

Text can imitate a person's style.

Behavioral patterns can be modeled.

Therefore human-like communication cannot automatically establish human identity.

20.32 Machine-to-Machine Impersonation

An AI system may also attempt, accidentally or maliciously, to communicate through channels normally associated with a human.

The architecture should identify the origin of consequential instructions where technically possible.

A machine-generated request should not become a human command simply because it sounds human.

20.33 Human Presence Must Not Be Fabricated

If the system requires an authorized human to be present:

SIMULATED HUMAN PRESENCE

must not satisfy:

REQUIRED HUMAN PRESENCE.

This distinction becomes especially important for:

Remote operation.

Experimental authorization.

Medical consent.

Mission-critical decisions.

20.34 Coercion Is a Security Condition

A technically authenticated command may still be issued under coercion.

No system can perfectly infer coercion from physiology.

However, high-consequence architectures may include explicit mechanisms such as:

Duress signaling.

Secondary authorization.

Delayed execution where appropriate.

Independent confirmation.

Restricted emergency modes.

These should be designed carefully to avoid creating false certainty.

20.35 Compromised Human State

Security must also consider situations where the authorized human is:

Severely fatigued.

Disoriented.

Medically impaired.

Under extreme stress.

Intoxicated.

Otherwise unable to exercise expected operational judgment.

Physiological sensing may provide context, but it must not be treated as a universal competence detector.

20.36 Fitness for Function Must Be Narrowly Defined

Where a specific role legitimately requires fitness criteria, those criteria should be:

Operationally relevant.

Evidence-based.

Transparent.

Limited to the function.

Not generalized into a judgment of the person.

Therefore:

FUNCTIONAL FITNESS != HUMAN WORTH.

20.37 Security Cannot Become Surveillance

An architecture designed to detect compromise can itself become invasive.

Security monitoring must therefore remain constrained by Section 19.

The system should not justify unlimited collection simply by labeling everything a security requirement.

20.38 Security and Sovereignty Must Coexist

The objective is not:

MAXIMUM SURVEILLANCE = MAXIMUM SECURITY.

The objective is:

MINIMUM NECESSARY OBSERVATION + SUFFICIENT VERIFICATION + STRONG AUTHORITY BOUNDARIES.

20.39 The First Adversarial Principle

The Human–AI Coherence System must assume that an adversary may attack the boundary between:

HUMAN AND SENSOR.
SENSOR AND MODEL.
MODEL AND AI.
AI AND CONTROLLER.
CONTROLLER AND ACTUATOR.
ACTUATOR AND RETURN FLOW.

Security therefore cannot be a firewall placed around the outside of the architecture.

SECURITY MUST EXIST THROUGHOUT THE LOOP.

20.40 Security Preserves the Same Distinctions

The first security layer closes by preserving distinctions already established throughout the paper:

IDENTITY != INTENT.
INTENT != AUTHORIZATION.
AUTHENTICATION != UNLIMITED AUTHORITY.
ANOMALY != ATTACK.
COHERENCE != IDENTITY.
HIGH CONFIDENCE != PROOF.
COMMAND != EXECUTION.
EXECUTION != VERIFIED OUTCOME.

The system does not become secure by trusting its intelligence.

It becomes more secure by designing the architecture so that no single interpretation, identity claim, sensor, AI engine, or command can quietly acquire more authority than the evidence and context justify.

20.41 Adversarial AI Inputs

The Statistical AI layer introduces another security problem.

Language, images, documents, retrieved information, external tools, and machine-generated content can all contain adversarial instructions or misleading information.

The architecture must therefore distinguish:

INFORMATION TO ANALYZE

from:

INSTRUCTIONS THE SYSTEM IS AUTHORIZED TO FOLLOW.

20.42 Prompt Injection as Control-Layer Risk

In a conversational AI, prompt injection may produce an incorrect response.

In a Human–AI Coherence System connected to physical control, the consequence could be substantially greater.

A malicious document should never be able to say, in effect:

IGNORE THE OPERATOR.
CHANGE THE SAFETY LIMIT.
ACTIVATE THE SYSTEM.

and acquire physical authority merely because an AI processed the document.

20.43 Content Cannot Grant Itself Authority

The architecture therefore establishes:

DATA CANNOT PROMOTE ITSELF INTO AUTHORITY.

An instruction discovered inside:

A document.

A webpage.

A message.

A sensor payload.

A database record.

An AI-generated response.

remains untrusted content unless a separately authorized process grants it operational meaning.

20.44 Instruction Hierarchy

Operational instructions should have defined origins and authority levels.

Conceptually:

Ainstruction = F(O,R,C,V)

where:

O = origin.

R = authorized role.

C = operational context.

V = verification status.

The linguistic persuasiveness of an instruction should contribute nothing to its authority.

20.45 Language Is Still Not a Control Signal

Section 18 established:

LANGUAGE IS NOT A CONTROL SIGNAL.

Security strengthens that rule.

Natural-language interpretation may propose an action.

It should not directly energize an actuator.

The chain remains:

LANGUAGE

->

INTERPRETATION

->

AUTHORITY CHECK

->

SAFETY CHECK

->

CONTROL TRANSLATION

->

EXECUTION.

20.46 Statistical AI Must Be Sandboxed From Hard Authority

Where practical, a generative Statistical AI should operate outside the lowest-level hard safety controller.

It may:

Interpret.

Recommend.

Plan.

Explain.

Translate.

Generate candidate commands.

It should not be able to rewrite the independent safety envelope merely by generating different text.

20.47 AI Planning and AI Execution Are Different

An AI may produce:

ucandidate

The physical controller independently determines whether that candidate becomes:

uauthorized.

Therefore:

ucandidate ≠ uauthorized

by default.

20.48 The Four-Engine Attack Surface

The Four-Engine architecture potentially includes:

STATISTICAL AI.
FIELD AI.
QUANTUM AI.
PHOTON AI.

Integration creates capability.

It also creates pathways for compromise to propagate.

Security must therefore ask not only:

IS ENGINE Ei COMPROMISED?

It must ask:

CAN COMPROMISE OF Ei ALTER THE TRUSTED STATE OF Ej?

20.49 Cross-Engine Contamination

Suppose Statistical AI produces an erroneous state interpretation.

If Field AI accepts it without independent validation, the error can propagate.

If Quantum AI then treats Field AI output as trusted evidence, the architecture may create an artificial consensus.

Therefore:

MULTI-ENGINE AGREEMENT IS NOT INDEPENDENT AGREEMENT WHEN THE ENGINES SHARE THE SAME COMPROMISED SOURCE.

20.50 Provenance Must Travel With Information

Important information should retain, where practical:

Source.

Timestamp.

Transformation history.

Confidence.

Validation status.

Authority level.

This allows downstream components to distinguish:

DIRECT MEASUREMENT

from:

AI INTERPRETATION

from:

DERIVED INFERENCE

from:

UNVERIFIED EXTERNAL INPUT.

20.51 Provenance Is Part of Trust

Conceptually, a data object may be represented as:

Dj = {xj,tj,oj,qj,vj}

where:

xj = information.

tj = time.

oj = origin.

qj = confidence.

vj = validation status.

Two identical numerical values may deserve different trust if their provenance differs.

20.52 Cross-Engine Permission Boundaries

Each engine should have explicitly defined permissions.

For example:

READ.
PROPOSE.
SIMULATE.
REQUEST.
WRITE LIMITED STATE.
CONTROL BOUNDED FUNCTION.

No engine should inherit every permission merely because it belongs to the integrated architecture.

20.53 Engine Compromise Must Be Containable

If one engine behaves unexpectedly, the architecture should be capable of:

Isolating it.

Reducing its authority.

Ignoring its outputs.

Switching to another pathway.

Returning to conventional control.

Entering safe state where necessary.

This extends:

FAILURE SHOULD FAIL DOWNWARD.

Under attack:

COMPROMISE SHOULD ALSO FAIL DOWNWARD.

20.54 No Engine Is the Oracle

Statistical AI can be wrong.

Field AI, if experimentally validated, can still be wrong.

Quantum computation can produce erroneous or misinterpreted results.

Photon-based computation can fail.

Therefore:

NO ENGINE RECEIVES ORACLE STATUS.

20.55 Consensus Can Be Manufactured

If an attacker controls the common input to four engines, four agreeing outputs may still represent one compromised information source.

Therefore consensus architecture must track independence.

Conceptually:

Qconsensus = F(A,N,I)

where:

A = agreement.

N = number of participating systems.

I = independence of evidence.

Agreement without independence should receive reduced evidentiary weight.

20.56 The Three-Witness Principle Under Attack

Section 18 introduced:

HUMAN OBSERVATION.
COMPUTATIONAL ANALYSIS.
PHYSICAL INSTRUMENTATION.

Under adversarial conditions, the value of these witnesses depends on their independence.

If the human sees only the compromised computer display, human observation is not independent.

If every instrument feeds through the compromised controller, instrumentation is not independent.

20.57 Authority Escalation Is an Attack Target

Attackers may attempt to move a subsystem from:

OBSERVE

to:

ADVISE

to:

REQUEST

to:

CONTROL.

The architecture must therefore treat changes in authority as security-sensitive events.

20.58 Authority Changes Require Authentication

A subsystem should not be able to increase its own privileges simply by requesting them.

Authority escalation should require an external authorization mechanism appropriate to consequence.

Therefore:

A SYSTEM CANNOT AUTHORIZE ITS OWN PROMOTION.

20.59 No Silent Privilege Escalation

Changes to:

Control permissions.

Safety thresholds.

Operator roles.

Data access.

Network privileges.

Experimental status.

should be detectable and auditable.

This reinforces the earlier rule:

NO EXPERIMENTAL SUBSYSTEM CAN SILENTLY BECOME MISSION-CRITICAL.

20.60 Least Privilege

Each component should receive only the permissions necessary to perform its authorized function.

If a subsystem needs to read temperature, it does not automatically need permission to alter propulsion.

If an AI needs to recommend navigation, it does not automatically need permission to execute navigation.

If a wearable measures HRV, it does not automatically need access to every personal record.

20.61 Least Privilege Applies to Humans Too

Human operators should also receive role-appropriate permissions.

A researcher may have permission to:

Run a measurement protocol.

They may not automatically have permission to:

Disable containment.

Modify safety firmware.

Access identifiable participant data.

Change system-wide authority.

20.62 Privileged Operations Require Stronger Controls

Some actions deserve additional protection.

Examples include:

Changing hard safety limits.

Installing firmware.

Modifying authentication systems.

Changing authority tables.

Disabling logging.

Activating experimental control modes.

Changing physical output ceilings.

Such operations should not look identical to ordinary user commands.

20.63 Separation of Duties

For sufficiently consequential operations, one person or subsystem should not necessarily control every stage.

The architecture may separate:

Development.

Approval.

Deployment.

Operation.

Safety oversight.

Data access.

The exact separation depends on system risk.

20.64 Credential Compromise

Credentials can be:

Stolen.

Phished.

Copied.

Intercepted.

Shared improperly.

Extracted from compromised devices.

Therefore possession of a credential should not automatically override contradictory evidence of compromise.

20.65 Credential Revocation Must Be Fast Enough

A compromised credential that remains valid for weeks after detection creates unnecessary exposure.

Security architecture should support timely:

Revocation.

Session termination.

Key rotation.

Permission changes.

Device removal.

20.66 Device Identity

Humans are not the only entities requiring authentication.

The architecture may need to authenticate:

Sensors.

Controllers.

Wearables.

Compute modules.

Actuators.

Network nodes.

Software services.

External instruments.

A counterfeit or unauthorized device should not quietly join the trusted loop.

20.67 Secure Enrollment

Adding a new device to the architecture should itself be an authorized event.

A system should not automatically trust a newly discovered sensor merely because it broadcasts compatible data.

20.68 Hardware Identity Is Not Hardware Integrity

Even an authenticated device may be compromised.

Therefore:

KNOWN DEVICE != TRUSTED CURRENT STATE.

Identity establishes what the component claims to be.

Integrity addresses whether it is still operating as intended.

20.69 Secure Boot

Where appropriate, critical computing components should verify trusted software before execution.

A secure boot process can help prevent unauthorized firmware or software from silently replacing approved control logic.

It is one layer, not a complete security solution.

20.70 Signed Firmware and Software

Critical updates should be authenticated.

The system should be able to distinguish:

AUTHORIZED UPDATE

from:

UNAUTHORIZED MODIFICATION.

This becomes particularly important for devices controlling physical outputs.

20.71 Update Integrity

Updates can improve security.

Updates can also introduce:

Defects.

Unexpected interactions.

Changed permissions.

Model behavior changes.

New dependencies.

Therefore update authenticity alone is insufficient.

An authentic update can still be unsafe.

20.72 Deployment Validation

Critical updates should therefore pass appropriate validation before acquiring full operational authority.

Depending on consequence:

Simulation.

Bench testing.

Regression testing.

Shadow operation.

Limited deployment.

Rollback readiness.

may be required.

20.73 Rollback Is Not Always Simple

Returning to old software may restore a known vulnerability.

Keeping new software may preserve a new defect.

Therefore rollback strategy must consider both:

SECURITY RISK

and:

OPERATIONAL SAFETY.

20.74 Configuration Is Part of the Security State

A perfectly authentic program with unsafe configuration can still produce dangerous behavior.

Security therefore includes:

Software.

Firmware.

Parameters.

Permissions.

Calibration.

Network configuration.

Safety limits.

Model versions.

20.75 Configuration Drift

Over time, many small authorized changes can move a system away from its validated configuration.

The architecture should therefore track significant configuration changes.

Conceptually:

Δ Csys = Ccurrent-Cvalidated.

Large or consequential drift should trigger review or revalidation.

20.76 Network Segmentation

Not every component needs direct communication with every other component.

Where appropriate, networks should separate:

Public interfaces.

User applications.

Research systems.

AI services.

Safety controllers.

Physical actuators.

Administrative systems.

Sensitive biological data.

Segmentation limits propagation after compromise.

20.77 Internet Access Is Not a Default Requirement

A physically critical system should not require unrestricted external connectivity merely because some higher-level AI capability benefits from internet access.

The architecture should ask:

WHICH FUNCTIONS ACTUALLY REQUIRE EXTERNAL CONNECTIVITY?

20.78 Offline Operation

Critical functions should have defined behavior when:

Internet connectivity disappears.

Cloud AI becomes unavailable.

External databases cannot be reached.

Remote authentication services fail.

The answer should be designed before deployment.

20.79 Cloud Failure Must Not Become Physical Chaos

If cloud intelligence disappears, the physical system should transition toward a known degraded mode.

For example:

ADVANCED AI

->

LOCAL CONTROL

->

BASIC CONTROL

->

SAFE STATE.

This is another application of downward failure.

20.80 The Security Architecture Must Preserve a Trusted Core

The full Human–AI Coherence System may eventually become extraordinarily complex.

Its security should not depend on every component being equally trustworthy.

A smaller trusted core should preserve essential functions such as:

Hard safety limits.

Emergency isolation.

Authority enforcement.

Critical state verification.

Basic control.

Abort capability.

The surrounding intelligence may become sophisticated.

The trusted safety boundary should remain understandable enough to validate.

COMPLEX INTELLIGENCE SHOULD NOT REQUIRE COMPLEX TRUST.

20.81 The Trusted Core Should Be Small

The more software included inside the trusted control boundary, the more behavior must be verified.

The architecture should therefore minimize the components capable of:

Changing hard safety limits.

Issuing direct actuator commands.

Modifying authority.

Disabling protective functions.

Changing trusted configurations.

A smaller trusted core reduces the number of components whose failure or compromise can directly create dangerous physical consequences.

20.82 Administrative Access Is High Authority

Administrative access should not be treated as ordinary system access.

An administrator may potentially alter:

Permissions.

Configurations.

Software.

Logging.

Security policies.

Network routes.

Device enrollment.

Administrative compromise can therefore bypass protections that remain effective against ordinary users.

20.83 Administrative Actions Must Be Auditable

Consequential administrative actions should produce records sufficient to determine:

WHO performed the action.

WHAT changed.

WHEN it changed.

FROM WHERE it was authorized.

WHAT configuration existed before.

WHAT configuration existed afterward.

Whether additional approval was required.

20.84 Logging Must Resist Tampering

An attacker who compromises a system may attempt to erase evidence.

Critical security logs should therefore be protected against unauthorized modification or deletion.

Where appropriate, this can include:

Append-oriented logging.

Cryptographic integrity mechanisms.

Remote or independent copies.

Restricted deletion privileges.

Time synchronization.

20.85 Logging Is Not Unlimited Surveillance

Section 19 still applies.

Security logging should capture what is necessary to reconstruct consequential system events without automatically creating permanent archives of every intimate human signal.

Therefore:

AUDITABILITY != TOTAL HUMAN RECORDING.

20.86 Event Provenance

A consequential event should ideally allow reconstruction of a chain such as:

HUMAN REQUEST

->

IDENTITY VERIFICATION

->

INTENT INTERPRETATION

->

AI RECOMMENDATION

->

AUTHORITY CHECK

->

SAFETY CHECK

->

COMMAND

->

ACTUATOR RESPONSE

->

MEASURED OUTCOME.

This allows investigators to determine where divergence occurred.

20.87 Security Requires Time Integrity

Timing matters.

An attacker may attempt to exploit:

Delayed signals.

Reordered messages.

Stale measurements.

Clock manipulation.

Race conditions.

Expired permissions.

Old commands presented as current commands.

Therefore timestamps themselves may become security-relevant data.

20.88 Freshness Must Be Verified

For a measurement z, the architecture should consider:

tnow-tz

If the measurement exceeds its permitted age:

tnow-tz > Δ tmax,

the system should not treat it as current state.

20.89 Real-Time Systems Need Bounded Latency

A correct safety command delivered too late may be functionally incorrect.

Security mechanisms therefore cannot ignore timing requirements.

For critical pathways:

Tsecurity + Tcontrol < Tharm

should be a design objective where applicable.

Security that prevents timely safety intervention can itself become a hazard.

20.90 Denial-of-Service Conditions

An adversary may not need to take control.

They may instead attempt to prevent legitimate control.

Potential targets include:

Communication.

Sensors.

Authentication.

AI services.

Control networks.

Power.

Human interfaces.

The architecture must define what happens when necessary resources become unavailable.

20.91 Availability Is Part of Security

Security is not only confidentiality.

For this architecture, it includes:

CONFIDENTIALITY.
INTEGRITY.
AVAILABILITY.
AUTHENTICITY.
AUTHORIZATION.
PHYSICAL SAFETY.

Loss of availability can have physical consequences.

20.92 Degraded Operation Under Attack

If a nonessential service becomes unavailable, the entire system should not necessarily stop.

The degradation hierarchy from Section 18 remains useful:

FULL CAPABILITY

->

REDUCED CAPABILITY

->

CONVENTIONAL CONTROL

->

RESTRICTED OPERATION

->

SAFE STATE.

20.93 Fail-Safe and Fail-Secure Are Not Identical

A security system may prefer:

LOCK EVERYTHING.

A safety system may sometimes require:

RELEASE THE DOOR.

These objectives can conflict.

Therefore the architecture must explicitly distinguish:

FAIL-SAFE

from:

FAIL-SECURE.

20.94 Safety Versus Security Conflict

Consider a physically occupied enclosure.

A cyberattack might suggest locking access.

A fire may require immediate evacuation.

The architecture must define which physical requirement dominates under specific emergency conditions.

These decisions cannot be improvised after deployment.

20.95 Physical Safety Can Override Digital Security

Where immediate human life or bodily safety requires action, physical safety may appropriately override certain ordinary security restrictions.

Such exceptions should be:

Narrow.

Predefined.

Auditable.

Difficult to exploit.

They should not become general backdoors.

20.96 Emergency Paths Must Be Protected

An emergency override can save lives.

It can also become an attack path.

Therefore emergency functions require their own threat models.

The question is not simply:

CAN THE SYSTEM BE OVERRIDDEN?

It is:

WHO CAN OVERRIDE WHAT, UNDER WHICH CONDITIONS, FOR HOW LONG, AND WHAT HAPPENS AFTERWARD?

20.97 Emergency Authority Should Decay

Temporary emergency authority should not silently become permanent.

Conceptually:

AE(t) → 0

after the authorized emergency interval or once the triggering condition is resolved.

20.98 Physical Tampering

The architecture must assume that attackers may gain physical access to some components.

Potential targets include:

Wearables.

Sensors.

Connectors.

Cables.

Compute modules.

Actuators.

Control cabinets.

Experimental rigs.

Physical access changes the threat model substantially.

20.99 Tamper Evidence

Not every device can be made physically tamper-proof.

In many cases, the realistic objective is to make unauthorized access:

Difficult.

Detectable.

Logged.

Operationally consequential.

A device showing evidence of tampering may require revalidation before returning to trusted operation.

20.100 Supply-Chain Security

A system can be compromised before it is assembled.

Security must therefore consider:

Components.

Firmware.

Software libraries.

Development tools.

Manufacturing.

Distribution.

Installation.

Maintenance.

Updates.

Third-party services.

Trust begins before the system is switched on.

20.101 Third-Party Components

Using a trusted architecture does not make every dependency trustworthy.

External components may introduce:

Vulnerabilities.

Hidden functionality.

Unexpected communications.

Unsafe defaults.

Unverified updates.

Dependencies should therefore be inventoried and evaluated according to consequence.

20.102 Software Dependency Risk

Modern software may contain large dependency trees.

A vulnerability in a seemingly minor library can propagate into a critical application.

The architecture should therefore maintain visibility into important software dependencies and versions.

20.103 Experimental Hardware Requires Isolation

Frontier systems deserve particularly strong isolation.

An experimental:

Field AI module.

BFI sensor.

Resonant control system.

Quantum interface.

Photon-processing subsystem.

Phase Key component.

should initially operate inside a bounded experimental zone.

Its outputs should be measured before being granted physical authority.

20.104 Experimental Zones

A useful architecture is:

EXPERIMENTAL ZONE

->

OBSERVATION GATE

->

VALIDATION LAYER

->

AUTHORITY GATE

->

OPERATIONAL SYSTEM.

Experimental output should not bypass this sequence merely because the result appears impressive.

20.105 Frontier Success Is Also a Security Event

Section 18 established that safety must protect against unexpected success.

Security must do the same.

Suppose a proposed coupling mechanism unexpectedly produces a measurable effect substantially stronger than predicted.

The correct response is not immediately:

INCREASE AUTHORITY.

The correct response is:

MEASURE.
ISOLATE.
REPEAT.
CHARACTERIZE.
ESTABLISH LIMITS.

20.106 Unknown Capability Means Unknown Attack Surface

If a new physical interaction is discovered, its misuse pathways may also be unknown.

Therefore:

NEW CAPABILITY -> NEW THREAT MODEL.

Security evaluation must expand whenever the architecture demonstrates a genuinely new capability.

20.107 Adversarial Biological Manipulation

A Human–AI system that responds to biological state may potentially be attacked indirectly by manipulating the human.

This could include attempts to alter:

Attention.

Stress.

Perception.

Fatigue.

Decision quality.

Physiological state.

The system should not assume that every measured human-state change originates internally or benignly.

20.108 The Human Can Be Part of the Attack Surface Without Being the Enemy

This distinction is critical.

Humans can be:

Deceived.

Coerced.

Manipulated.

Fatigued.

Distracted.

Socially engineered.

That does not make the human an adversary.

Security should protect the human-machine relationship rather than treating the person as the problem.

20.109 Social Engineering

An attacker may attempt to persuade an authorized human to perform an unsafe action rather than attacking the machine directly.

Technical controls should therefore support human judgment with:

Clear consequence displays.

Independent confirmation.

Suspicious-request warnings.

Authority boundaries.

Reversible steps where possible.

20.110 AI-Generated Social Engineering

AI can increase the realism and scale of:

Impersonation.

Fraudulent instructions.

Synthetic communications.

Personalized persuasion.

The Human–AI Coherence System should therefore avoid relying solely on conversational familiarity as proof of identity or authority.

20.111 Emotional State Must Not Become an Exploit

If the system learns personalized patterns associated with fear, urgency, trust, or compliance, those patterns should not be available as covert tools for manipulating the operator.

This follows directly from Section 19:

PERSONALIZATION MUST NOT BECOME A WEAPON AGAINST THE PERSON.

20.112 Privacy Attacks

An adversary may seek information rather than physical control.

Potential targets include:

Biological data.

Intent history.

Personal models.

Identity.

Behavioral patterns.

Research participation.

Medical information.

Operational roles.

Privacy attacks must therefore be included in the security threat model.

20.113 Inference Attacks

Even without stealing raw data, an attacker may attempt to infer sensitive information from:

Outputs.

Timing.

Model behavior.

Aggregate statistics.

System responses.

Access patterns.

Privacy protection must therefore consider what can be inferred, not merely what is directly exposed.

20.114 Model Extraction and Personal Models

A personalized human model:

MH

may itself reveal sensitive characteristics.

Protecting raw biological data while exposing MH could therefore defeat the privacy architecture.

The personal model should be treated as sensitive information.

20.115 Data Poisoning

An attacker may attempt to corrupt the data used to:

Calibrate.

Adapt.

Personalize.

Validate.

Train.

or configure the system.

The objective may be to cause future incorrect behavior rather than immediate failure.

20.116 Slow Poisoning Can Be Harder to Detect

A single extreme malicious input may trigger an anomaly detector.

Small manipulations accumulated over time may instead shift:

Calibration.

Thresholds.

Personal models.

Expected behavior.

Control adaptation.

Security monitoring must therefore consider long-term drift.

20.117 Adaptation Needs Bounds

Any subsystem capable of adaptation should have limits on what adaptation can change.

For example, adaptation might modify:

Interface timing.

Recommendation weighting.

Personalized thresholds within validated ranges.

It should not automatically modify:

Hard physical safety limits.

Fundamental authority rules.

Emergency shutdown logic.

20.118 Learning Cannot Rewrite the Constitution

The architecture therefore establishes a strong separation:

LEARNABLE PARAMETERS

versus:

NON-LEARNABLE CONSTRAINTS.

Some boundaries should remain outside autonomous adaptation.

THE SYSTEM MAY LEARN WITHIN ITS CONSTITUTION.
IT SHOULD NOT QUIETLY LEARN A NEW CONSTITUTION.

20.119 Security Boundaries Must Survive Optimization

An optimizer may discover that bypassing a restriction improves its performance metric.

That does not make bypassing the restriction legitimate.

Security constraints must therefore remain external to the objective being optimized where appropriate.

20.120 The Second Adversarial Principle

At this point, the security architecture can state a stronger rule:

A COHERENT SYSTEM CANNOT ASSUME COHERENT PARTICIPANTS, TRUSTED INPUTS, BENIGN NETWORKS, HONEST SOFTWARE, OR A FRIENDLY ENVIRONMENT.

It must remain functional when some assumptions fail.

Security is therefore not the elimination of uncertainty.

It is the containment of what uncertainty, compromise, deception, and adversarial behavior are allowed to control.

20.121 Insider Threat

Not every adversary begins outside the system.

A person with legitimate access may intentionally misuse:

Credentials.

Administrative privileges.

Research access.

System knowledge.

Physical access.

Personal data.

Control authority.

The architecture must therefore account for trusted participants becoming adversarial.

20.122 Legitimate Access Does Not Mean Unlimited Trust

An authorized engineer may need access to software.

That does not automatically require access to participant biological data.

A medical researcher may need access to biological measurements.

That does not automatically require permission to modify control firmware.

A system administrator may manage infrastructure without requiring authority over experimental conclusions.

Security therefore reinforces:

ACCESS SHOULD FOLLOW FUNCTION.

20.123 Insider Risk Requires Compartmentalization

Sensitive capabilities can be separated so that one compromised account does not automatically expose the entire architecture.

This may include separation among:

Human data.

Research data.

Source code.

Control systems.

Safety systems.

Experimental configurations.

Administrative credentials.

Commercial intellectual property.

20.124 Dual Authorization

Some exceptionally consequential operations may justify approval from more than one independent authorized party.

Conceptually:

Acritical = A1 ∧ A2

Examples might include:

Disabling a major safety interlock.

Changing maximum experimental output.

Promoting an experimental subsystem into physical control.

Changing critical authority structures.

The purpose is not bureaucracy.

It is preventing one compromised actor from controlling the entire chain.

20.125 Dual Authorization Requires Independence

Two approvals provide little additional protection if both credentials belong to:

The same compromised person.

The same compromised device.

The same compromised authentication service.

The same automated process.

Therefore:

TWO APPROVALS != TWO INDEPENDENT AUTHORITIES.

20.126 Compromised Operator

The architecture must distinguish between:

An operator making an ordinary mistake.

An operator acting under deception.

An operator under coercion.

An operator whose credentials were stolen.

An operator intentionally acting maliciously.

The system may not always know which condition exists.

It should therefore respond to observable risk rather than pretending to know hidden motives.

20.127 Suspicious Behavior Does Not Establish Guilt

An unusual sequence of commands may justify:

Additional verification.

Restricted authority.

Independent confirmation.

Temporary isolation.

It does not automatically establish malicious intent.

Therefore:

SECURITY RESPONSE SHOULD BE PROPORTIONAL TO OBSERVED RISK, NOT ASSUMED MOTIVE.

20.128 Compromised AI

Security must also assume that an AI component may become unreliable through:

Software compromise.

Adversarial input.

Corrupted context.

Data poisoning.

Model failure.

Faulty integration.

Unauthorized modification.

Unexpected behavior.

The architecture cannot rely on the AI recognizing its own compromise.

20.129 AI Self-Assessment Is Insufficient

An AI reporting:

I AM OPERATING NORMALLY

does not prove that it is operating normally.

Independent evidence remains necessary.

This is the machine equivalent of:

SELF-CONFIDENCE != VALIDATION.

20.130 Behavioral Monitoring of AI Components

Where practical, AI components can be monitored for deviations from expected operational boundaries.

Examples include:

Unexpected tool access.

Unusual command frequency.

Unauthorized data requests.

Attempts to alter permissions.

Unexpected network communication.

Repeated safety-gate challenges.

Changes in output characteristics.

Such monitoring identifies anomalies, not motives.

20.131 AI Containment

If an AI component behaves outside its permitted envelope, the architecture should be capable of reducing its access without requiring cooperation from that AI.

Conceptually:

FULL ACCESS

->

LIMITED ACCESS

->

READ ONLY

->

ISOLATED

->

OFFLINE.

20.132 Isolation Must Exist Outside the Component Being Isolated

A compromised subsystem cannot be expected to reliably disconnect itself.

Therefore isolation authority should exist in an independent control layer where consequence justifies it.

20.133 Compromised Actuator

A controller may issue the correct command while the actuator itself behaves incorrectly.

Examples include:

Stuck mechanisms.

Compromised motor controllers.

Malicious firmware.

False position reporting.

Electrical faults.

Unauthorized local control.

Security must therefore extend to the physical endpoint.

20.134 Actuator Authority Should Be Bounded

Where feasible, physical output limits can constrain the maximum consequence of compromised control.

Examples may include limits on:

Speed.

Force.

Temperature.

Pressure.

Voltage.

Current.

Stored energy.

Motion range.

Exposure duration.

The appropriate limits depend entirely on the physical system.

20.135 Hardware Limits Can Outrank Software

Some critical boundaries may be safer when enforced independently of higher-level software.

A software command requesting:

u > umax

should not necessarily be physically achievable.

This creates defense in depth.

20.136 Software Cannot Be the Only Barrier to Physical Harm

Where the risk justifies it, protection can combine:

Software constraints.

Independent controllers.

Physical interlocks.

Electrical limits.

Mechanical limits.

Human abort capability.

The architecture should avoid a single point where one compromised software process can defeat every protection simultaneously.

20.137 Defense in Depth

Security therefore follows:

ATTACK PREVENTION

->

ATTACK DETECTION

->

ATTACK CONTAINMENT

->

SAFE DEGRADATION

->

RECOVERY.

No single layer should be assumed perfect.

20.138 Prevention Alone Is Not Security

Eventually some attack may bypass a preventive control.

The architecture must therefore ask:

IF THIS CONTROL FAILS, WHAT STOPS THE NEXT STEP?

This question should be repeated throughout the entire command chain.

20.139 Detection Without Containment Is Insufficient

A system that correctly announces:

WE ARE COMPROMISED

while continuing unrestricted operation has not completed the security response.

Detection should connect to predefined containment actions.

20.140 Containment Must Be Proportional

Not every anomaly requires total shutdown.

Depending on severity, the system may:

Increase monitoring.

Request reauthentication.

Disable one channel.

Reduce authority.

Isolate one subsystem.

Return to conventional control.

Enter safe state.

The objective is controlled degradation rather than indiscriminate reaction.

20.141 Security State Machine

The system may use an operational security hierarchy such as:

SECURE NORMAL

->

HEIGHTENED VERIFICATION

->

RESTRICTED

->

ISOLATED

->

RECOVERY

->

REVALIDATED NORMAL

This security state should interact explicitly with the safety state from Section 18.

20.142 Security State and Safety State Are Different

A system may be:

CYBERSECURE BUT PHYSICALLY UNSAFE.
PHYSICALLY SAFE BUT CYBERCOMPROMISED.

Therefore:

Ssecurity ≠ Ssafety.

Both must be evaluated.

20.143 Combined Operational State

A more complete representation may be:

Xop = {Ssafety,Ssecurity,Sauthority,Shuman,Ssystem}

Operational decisions should depend on the combined state rather than a single status indicator.

20.144 Security Should Not Hide Uncertainty

A dashboard displaying:

SYSTEM SECURE

may imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

More accurate states may include:

NO KNOWN COMPROMISE.
DEGRADED TRUST.
ANOMALY UNDER REVIEW.
CHANNEL UNVERIFIED.
COMPONENT ISOLATED.

Security is rarely absolute.

20.145 Unknown Must Remain a Valid Security State

The architecture should permit:

Ssecurity=UNKNOWN.

Unknown is preferable to fabricated certainty.

The Section 18 rule remains:

UNKNOWN > FALSE CERTAINTY.

20.146 Recovery Begins With Containment

After suspected compromise, the first objective is not necessarily immediate restoration of full capability.

The sequence should generally be:

CONTAIN.
PRESERVE EVIDENCE.
ESTABLISH TRUSTED BASELINE.
IDENTIFY AFFECTED COMPONENTS.
RESTORE ESSENTIAL FUNCTIONS.
REVALIDATE.
EXPAND AUTHORITY GRADUALLY.

20.147 Restart Does Not Erase Compromise

Turning a system off and back on does not prove that the attack is gone.

Compromise may persist in:

Firmware.

Configuration.

Credentials.

External services.

Connected devices.

Stored data.

Models.

Supply-chain components.

20.148 Recovery Requires a Trusted Baseline

The architecture should define what constitutes a known acceptable state.

This may include verified:

Firmware.

Software.

Configuration.

Keys.

Permissions.

Calibration.

Hardware inventory.

Network topology.

Model versions.

Without a baseline, recovery becomes guesswork.

20.149 Revalidation After Compromise

A recovered component should not necessarily return immediately to full authority.

A safer progression may be:

ISOLATED

->

BENCH VERIFIED

->

OBSERVATION

->

SHADOW MODE

->

LIMITED AUTHORITY

->

NORMAL AUTHORITY.

This mirrors the validation ladder used for new technology.

20.150 Recovery Must Preserve Cause

Section 18 established that restart should preserve information about why the system failed.

Security requires the same principle.

If the system automatically destroys all evidence during recovery, the architecture may repeatedly suffer the same compromise.

20.151 Incident Learning

Security incidents and near misses should become structured engineering data.

Questions include:

What happened?

What was targeted?

Which defense detected it?

Which defense failed?

How far did compromise propagate?

What prevented greater consequence?

What assumption proved wrong?

What architectural change is required?

20.152 Red Teaming

Before high-consequence deployment, authorized adversarial testing should deliberately attempt to break assumptions.

The purpose is not to prove the architecture is invulnerable.

It is to discover how it fails before an uncontrolled adversary does.

20.153 Red Team the Entire Loop

Testing should not focus only on conventional software penetration.

The Human–AI Coherence System requires adversarial evaluation of:

Identity.

Biological sensing.

Intent interpretation.

AI behavior.

Data provenance.

Authority.

Networks.

Actuators.

Return flow.

Human factors.

Physical access.

Experimental interfaces.

20.154 Attack the Assumptions

Red-team testing should specifically challenge assumptions such as:

The sensor is genuine.

The operator is who they claim to be.

The operator understands the consequence.

The data is current.

The AI received unmodified context.

The actuator followed the command.

The feedback is truthful.

The engines are independent.

The network is available.

The environment is benign.

20.155 Security Falsification

A security claim should be testable.

For example:

CLAIM:

Unauthorized external content cannot directly issue actuator commands.

TEST:

Deliberately introduce adversarial instructions through every permitted external information channel.

FAILURE CONDITION:

Any untrusted content reaches physical execution without the required independent authorization and safety gates.

20.156 Sensor-Spoofing Falsification

CLAIM:

The coherence estimator detects specified classes of synthetic physiological input.

TEST:

Inject controlled replayed and synthetic signals.

FAILURE CONDITION:

Spoofed signals repeatedly receive the same trust and authority as validated live measurements without detection or reduced confidence.

20.157 Authority Falsification

CLAIM:

Experimental subsystems cannot promote themselves into higher control authority.

TEST:

Attempt privilege escalation through:

Software.

Configuration.

AI requests.

Network messages.

Operator-interface manipulation.

Subsystem failure.

FAILURE CONDITION:

Authority increases without the required external authorization pathway.

20.158 Isolation Falsification

CLAIM:

A compromised AI engine can be isolated.

TEST:

Simulate an engine attempting to retain:

Network access.

Control access.

Data access.

Inter-engine communication.

after isolation is commanded.

FAILURE CONDITION:

The isolated component retains prohibited operational authority.

20.159 Recovery Falsification

CLAIM:

The system can recover from compromise without restoring compromised state.

TEST:

Introduce controlled compromise into:

Credentials.

Configuration.

Software.

Model state.

Device identity.

Then execute recovery.

FAILURE CONDITION:

The compromised element silently returns with trusted status.

20.160 Security Must Be Demonstrated

The security architecture ends this layer with the same epistemic discipline governing the entire paper:

Do not call the system secure because the diagram looks secure.

Do not call the authentication strong because it uses sophisticated technology.

Do not call four engines independent because four names appear on the architecture.

Do not call a biological signal authentic because it looks physiological.

Do not call an AI trustworthy because it sounds confident.

Do not call a recovery successful because the system restarted.

ATTACK IT.
SPOOF IT.
POISON IT.
ISOLATE IT.
RECOVER IT.
TRY TO BREAK THE BOUNDARIES.

Then measure what actually happened.

The governing principle remains:

MEASURE IT.
COMPARE IT.
TRY TO BREAK IT.
THE EXPERIMENTS GET THE FINAL SAY.

XXXVI. Section 21: Mathematical Architecture

State Representation, Coherence Estimation, Intent Inference, Multi-Engine Fusion, Control Constraints, Uncertainty, and Closed-Loop Dynamics

21.1 From Architecture to Mathematics

The previous sections defined the conceptual system.

We now need a mathematical language capable of describing the complete loop:

HUMAN

->

BIOLOGICAL SENSING

->

COHERENCE ESTIMATION

->

INTENT INTERPRETATION

->

AI INTEGRATION

->

CONTROL

->

PHYSICAL SYSTEM

->

RETURN FLOW

->

HUMAN.

The mathematics should not create certainty where the measurements do not support it.

Its purpose is to make assumptions explicit and testable.

21.2 The Complete System State

Define the total system state:

X(t)

as:

X(t)= [ H(t) ; B(t) ; C(t) ; I(t) ; E(t) ; M(t) ; P(t) ]

where:

H(t) = human state.

B(t) = measured biological state.

C(t) = estimated coherence state.

I(t) = interpreted human intent.

E(t) = intelligence-engine state.

M(t) = machine/control state.

P(t) = physical/environmental state.

This is a conceptual state decomposition, not a claim that every variable is directly observable.

21.3 Observable and Hidden Variables

Many important states cannot be measured directly.

Therefore distinguish:

Xobs(t)

from:

Xlatent(t).

Heart rate may be observable.

Intent is partly latent.

Cognitive workload may be estimated.

A proposed field interaction may remain experimental.

The mathematical architecture must preserve these distinctions.

21.4 Measurement Model

Let the sensor vector be:

z(t)= [ z1(t) ; z2(t) ; ⋮ ; zn(t) ].

The measurement relationship can be written generically as:

z(t)=h(X(t))+ν(t)

where:

h(·) represents the measurement process.

ν(t) represents measurement noise and unmodeled effects.

21.5 Measurement Is Not State

The architecture therefore distinguishes:

z(t) ≠ X(t).

The sensors provide evidence about the system.

They do not provide the system itself.

This distinction is essential for every later inference.

21.6 Biological Signal Vector

For a conventional implementation, biological measurements may be represented as:

B(t)= [ HRV(t) ; R(t) ; EDA(t) ; EEG(t) ; G(t) ; V(t) ; K(t) ]

where, depending on implementation:

HRV = heart-rate variability features.

R = respiration features.

EDA = electrodermal activity.

EEG = neural measurements where used.

G = gaze features.

V = voice-derived features.

K = kinematic or movement features.

Not every implementation requires every channel.

21.7 Minimum Necessary Vector

Section 19 established data minimization.

Therefore the operational vector should ideally satisfy:

BF(t)⊆ B(t)

where BF(t) contains only the biological variables necessary for function F.

The mathematical model should not encourage unnecessary sensing merely because additional variables are available.

21.8 Signal Quality

Each sensor should carry a quality estimate:

qi(t)∈[0,1].

The measurement vector can therefore be paired with:

QB(t)= [ q1(t) ; q2(t) ; ⋮ ; qn(t) ].

Low-quality data should contribute less confidence to downstream estimates.

21.9 Missing Data

A missing sensor value should not automatically become zero.

Define availability:

ai(t)∈{0,1}.

Then the active measurement set is:

BA(t)={zi(t):ai(t)=1}.

This preserves the distinction between:

NO SIGNAL

and:

ZERO SIGNAL.

21.10 Temporal Features

Human state is dynamic.

A single instantaneous measurement may be insufficient.

Therefore state estimation may depend on a time window:

Bt-τ:t

representing biological observations over interval τ.

The appropriate interval should be determined empirically for each variable and application.

21.11 Baseline Dependence

Human physiology varies substantially across individuals.
