LXXII. Appendix N: Citation and Source Integrity Audit

N.1 Purpose

The reference architecture of Human–AI Coherence Systems is part of its evidence architecture.

A citation does more than identify prior work.

Its placement can imply:

  • provenance;
  • precedent;
  • methodological support;
  • empirical support;
  • theoretical support;
  • independent replication;
  • validation.

Those implications are not equivalent.

The manuscript therefore adopts:

CITED ≠ VALIDATED.

and:

SOURCE STRENGTH ≥ CLAIM STRENGTH ATTRIBUTED TO THAT SOURCE.

N.2 Three Source Classes

Every significant technical proposition should be understood relative to one of three source classes.

Established External Literature

LE = ESTABLISHED EXTERNAL LITERATURE

This category includes independent literature concerning:

  • psychophysiology;
  • HRV;
  • EDA;
  • EEG;
  • BCI;
  • multimodal sensing;
  • human factors;
  • adaptive automation;
  • human–AI interaction;
  • trust in automation;
  • control theory;
  • nonlinear dynamics;
  • coupled oscillators;
  • reservoir computing;
  • physical reservoir computing;
  • analog and neuromorphic computing;
  • photonic computing;
  • quantum computing;
  • cybersecurity;
  • runtime assurance;
  • research methodology;
  • human-subject protection;
  • metrology and measurement uncertainty.

These sources establish scientific and engineering context.

They do not automatically validate the Christos systems that incorporate those components.

Christos Framework Sources

LC = CHRISTOS FRAMEWORK SOURCES

This category documents internal architectural ancestry, including relevant work concerning:

  • Christfield Dynamics;
  • coherence frameworks;
  • Coherence Bridge;
  • Field AI;
  • RCE/RCM architectures;
  • Four-Engine integration;
  • Hearthstone;
  • HACS;
  • Phase Key;
  • transportation;
  • Echo Pod;
  • Aether Skiff;
  • Sovereign Explorer Vessel;
  • associated control and physical-system architectures.

These sources establish:

PROVENANCE.

They do not automatically establish:

INDEPENDENT VALIDATION.

Hypotheses Introduced in This Work

LH = HYPOTHESES INTRODUCED IN THIS WORK.

Where a proposition originates in Human–AI Coherence Systems, it should be identified as:

PROPOSED HERE.

An unrelated external citation should not be attached merely to make the proposition appear established.

Therefore:

NO CITATION > MISLEADING CITATION.

N.3 The Evidence Firewall Applies to References

The manuscript already distinguishes:

ESTABLISHED | CHRISTOS ENGINEERING | EXPERIMENTAL | FRONTIER.

The reference system must preserve the same boundary.

A citation cannot move a claim from one category to another merely through proximity.

For example:

A=established

and:

A⊂ B

does not imply:

B=established.

The valid relationship is:

Aestablished + Bproposed → Btestable using A.

N.4 Physiological Measurement Boundary

External literature can support the proposition:

ECG, PPG, HRV, RESP, EDA, EEG, EMG, AND MOTION CAN BE MEASURED.

It can support established acquisition and analysis methods.

It may support known physiological interpretations within the limits of those literatures.

It does not independently establish:

CCI=VALID MEASURE OF HUMAN COHERENCE.

Therefore:

HRV⊂ XH

may be externally grounded.

But:

HRV=CCI

or:

HRV=CH

must not be implied.

N.5 Multimodal State Estimation Boundary

External literature may establish that multiple sensor channels can be combined to estimate aspects of human state.

This supports the general architecture:

{ x1,…,xn } → FEATURES → STATE ESTIMATE.

It does not independently establish that the specific Christos state representation is optimal.

It does not establish that CCI adds predictive information beyond simpler models.

That remains a testable Christos proposition.

N.6 BCI Boundary

Brain–computer interface literature supports:

MEASURED BIOLOGICAL SIGNAL → INTERPRETATION → EXTERNAL ACTION.

It does not support:

UNMEASURED INTENTION → DIRECT PHYSICAL ACTION.

Therefore BCI literature must never be positioned as validation of direct Human–Field coupling.

N.7 Human–Automation Boundary

External human-factors and automation literature supports:

  • different levels of automation;
  • human–automation coordination;
  • automation bias;
  • trust calibration;
  • shared control;
  • human oversight;
  • appropriate reliance.

It provides strong precedent for:

CAPABILITY ≠ AUTHORITY.

However, the principle:

HUMAN PURPOSE > MACHINE PROCEDURE

is a governing design principle of this architecture.

It should not be presented as an externally discovered scientific law.

N.8 Nonlinear-Dynamics Boundary

External literature supports:

  • oscillators;
  • nonlinear dynamics;
  • phase relationships;
  • coupling;
  • synchronization;
  • collective behavior;
  • attractors.

It therefore provides legitimate mathematical precedent for studying RCE/RCM dynamics.

It does not establish:

RCM16=INTELLIGENT COMPUTATIONAL SUBSTRATE.

The manuscript must preserve:

OSCILLATION → COUPLING → DYNAMICS

before experimentally establishing:

INFORMATION → COMPUTATION → UTILITY.

N.9 Reservoir-Computing Boundary

Reservoir-computing literature supports the proposition that recurrent dynamical systems can transform temporal inputs into states useful for computation.

Physical-reservoir literature further establishes that:

PHYSICAL DYNAMICS CAN PARTICIPATE IN COMPUTATION.

This makes physical reservoir computing an appropriate comparison class for Field AI.

It does not establish:

FIELD AI COMPUTES.

That requires Field AI experiments.

The correct research comparison is:

RCM ↔ PRCestablished.

N.10 Field AI Must Earn Its Own Computational Citation Chain

If future Field AI experiments demonstrate computational performance, those experimental reports become the direct sources supporting that claim.

The chain then becomes:

LE → COMPARISON CLASS
LC → ARCHITECTURAL PROVENANCE
FIELD AI EXPERIMENT → DIRECT EVIDENCE.

This is stronger than attempting to use reservoir-computing literature as indirect proof.

N.11 Photonic Boundary

External photonic-computing literature supports:

PHOTONIC COMPUTATION EXISTS.

It may support particular established photonic operations, architectures, devices, and performance characteristics.

It does not establish:

CHRISTOS PHOTON AI IS VALIDATED.

The Christos implementation receives its own evidence ledger.

N.12 Quantum Boundary

External quantum-computing literature supports:

QUANTUM COMPUTATION EXISTS.

It does not establish:

CHRISTOS QUANTUM AI IS VALIDATED.

Nor does quantum literature establish that a Four-Engine system benefits from including a quantum engine for every task.

Task-specific advantage must be demonstrated.

N.13 Four-Engine Boundary

Literature on ensemble methods and heterogeneous computing may provide precedent for combining computational systems.

It does not establish that the specific Four-Engine architecture:

{ Statistical, Field, Photon, Quantum }

is superior.

That is a Christos engineering proposition.

Likewise:

ENGINE DIVERSITY ≠ EVIDENCE INDEPENDENCE.

No external ensemble citation should be allowed to erase that distinction.

N.14 Cybersecurity Boundary

External cybersecurity and zero-trust literature can support:

  • authentication;
  • authorization;
  • least privilege;
  • segmentation;
  • provenance;
  • secure communications;
  • access control;
  • explicit trust boundaries.

It supports the engineering principle:

REQUEST ≠ AUTHORIZATION.

It does not independently validate HACS as an industry standard.

HACS remains:

A PROPOSED CHRISTOS INTEROPERABILITY AND GOVERNANCE STANDARD.

N.15 Human-Subject and Privacy Boundary

External ethical and regulatory literature can support:

  • informed consent;
  • human-subject protection;
  • data minimization;
  • privacy;
  • risk management;
  • research oversight.

It does not establish the validity of a particular human-state interpretation.

Thus:

ETHICALLY COLLECTED DATA ≠ CORRECT INTERPRETATION.

Both requirements matter.

N.16 Metrology Boundary

Measurement-science literature supports:

  • uncertainty estimation;
  • calibration;
  • traceability;
  • measurement models;
  • error analysis.

This is particularly important for frontier experiments.

Metrology can establish whether an instrument has measured a quantity within specified uncertainty.

It cannot, by itself, identify the mechanism producing that quantity.

Therefore:

MEASURED ANOMALY ≠ NEW PHYSICS.

N.17 Phase Key Citation Boundary

External literature may support the conventional behavior of:

  • oscillators;
  • resonant circuits;
  • coils;
  • crystals;
  • plasma devices;
  • electromagnetic systems;
  • acoustic systems;
  • sensors;
  • signal processing.

Those sources may establish how conventional components behave.

They do not establish:

  • direct intention-dependent coupling;
  • unconventional state selection;
  • frontier navigation effects;
  • nonconventional physical transitions.

The correct structure is:

KNOWN COMPONENT PHYSICS + CHRISTOS CONFIGURATION + CONTROLLED EXPERIMENT → RESULT.

Not:

KNOWN COMPONENT PHYSICS → FRONTIER CLAIM VALIDATED.

N.18 Propulsion Citation Boundary

Established literature can support:

  • force measurement;
  • thermal artifacts;
  • vibration;
  • airflow;
  • outgassing;
  • electrostatic interaction;
  • electromagnetic interaction;
  • magnetic interaction;
  • mechanical relaxation;
  • measurement uncertainty;
  • conventional propulsion physics.

Such literature is particularly valuable for identifying alternative explanations.

It must not be used to imply that an unconventional propulsion mechanism exists.

The evidence sequence remains experimental:

FORCE → REPEATABILITY → ARTIFACT CONTROL → REPLICATION → CONTROL → SCALING → PROPULSION.

N.19 Transportation Citation Boundary

External literature can support:

  • vehicle control;
  • shared control;
  • human factors;
  • navigation;
  • fault tolerance;
  • runtime assurance;
  • hardware-in-the-loop methods;
  • vehicle safety.

Christos sources establish provenance for:

  • Echo Pod;
  • Aether Skiff;
  • associated Human–AI vehicle architecture.

Neither source class establishes an untested frontier propulsion mechanism.

Therefore:

VEHICLE ARCHITECTURE SOURCE ≠ PROPULSION EVIDENCE.

N.20 SEV Citation Boundary

The SEV combines subsystems with different evidence states.

Its citations must therefore attach to subsystems and claims rather than treating the vessel as one evidentiary object.

For example:

  • Human factors: external human-factors sources.
  • Control architecture: external control literature + Christos architecture provenance.
  • Field AI: external physical-computing comparison + Christos provenance + direct Field AI experiments when available.
  • Frontier propulsion: direct propulsion experiments when available.
  • Direct intention-dependent navigation: dedicated controlled experiments.

No citation to one subsystem validates the whole vessel.

N.21 Christos Cross-Citation Rule

Christos papers may cite other Christos papers to document architecture development.

For example:

Christfield Dynamics → Coherence Bridge → HACS.

That establishes an intellectual and engineering lineage.

It does not create multiple independent witnesses.

Therefore:

DOCUMENT COUNT ≠ EVIDENCE COUNT.

and:

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY ≠ EXTERNAL VALIDATION.

N.22 Repetition Does Not Create Replication

Suppose the same proposition appears in:

P1,P2,P3,P4.

If all four papers inherit the proposition from the same original source or dataset, the evidence does not become:

n=4.

It remains one evidence lineage unless independently tested.

Therefore provenance should identify:

  • originating proposition;
  • inherited use;
  • direct experiment;
  • replication source.

N.23 Contradictory Literature Must Be Included

The reference architecture should not function as a collection of supportive quotations.

Where substantial competing explanations exist, they should be represented.

This is especially important for:

  • biological coherence interpretations;
  • physiological inference;
  • consciousness-related interpretation;
  • unconventional sensing;
  • intention-dependent effects;
  • anomalous forces;
  • unconventional propulsion.

The correct scientific question is not:

What literature supports the architecture?

It is:

WHAT DOES THE TOTAL RELEVANT EVIDENCE REQUIRE US TO CONCLUDE?

N.24 Competing Explanations Are Part of the Experiment

For frontier claims, contradictory or conventional literature can improve experimental design.

If literature identifies:

  • thermal drift;
  • vibration;
  • airflow;
  • electrostatics;
  • magnetic forces;
  • cable forces;
  • sensor artifacts;
  • expectation effects;
  • movement contamination;
  • signal leakage;

those are not obstacles to the experiment.

They become:

CONTROL VARIABLES.

A strong frontier experiment actively attempts to reproduce its apparent effect through conventional confounds.

If a confound reproduces the signal, the experiment has learned something.

N.25 Direct Evidence Outranks Analogy

The manuscript uses legitimate analogies and comparison classes.

However:

ANALOGY < DIRECT MEASUREMENT.

For example:

Physical reservoir computing may motivate Field AI.

It cannot replace Field AI benchmarking.

BCI may motivate Human–AI biological interfaces.

It cannot replace validation of the Coherence Bridge.

Conventional resonant systems may motivate Phase Key experiments.

They cannot replace Phase Key experiments.

N.26 Source-to-Claim Ledger

For important claims, maintain:

Ci → { S1,S2,…,Sn }.

Each mapping should include:

FieldMeaning
Claim IDClaim being supported
Claim classEF / CEP / EXP / F
SourceSupporting reference
Source classL_E, L_C, or direct experiment
Support typeBackground, method, precedent, provenance, direct evidence, replication
Support strengthExact scope of what the source establishes
LimitWhat the source does not establish

This ledger need not appear in full in the main published paper.

It should exist as part of the research record.

N.27 Example Source-to-Claim Mapping

Claim: HRV can be measured and analyzed using established methods.

Class: EF. Source: external HRV methodological literature. Support: direct established methodological foundation.

Claim: CCI provides information beyond HRV and simpler multimodal baselines.

Class: EXP. Source: future direct CCI experiment. Support required: incremental predictive validity.

External HRV literature does not establish this claim.

Claim: Coupled oscillators can exhibit synchronization.

Class: EF. Source: nonlinear-dynamics literature.

Claim: RCM16 performs useful computation.

Class: EXP. Source required: direct RCM benchmark experiment.

Coupled-oscillator literature does not establish this claim.

Claim: Physical systems can implement reservoir computation.

Class: EF. Source: physical-reservoir-computing literature.

Claim: Field AI outperforms established physical reservoirs for task T.

Class: EXP. Source required: controlled comparative benchmark.

Claim: Direct intention-dependent physical coupling exists.

Class: F. Source required: preregistered, controlled, independently replicated direct experiment.

BCI literature does not establish this claim.

Claim: A proposed propulsion system generates useful controllable force.

Class: EXP/F depending on mechanism. Source required: direct force experiment, artifact controls, replication, and scaling.

Vehicle-design documents do not establish this claim.

N.28 Citation Placement Rule

Place a citation immediately after the proposition it actually supports.

Avoid constructing a paragraph in which:

  • 1. an established fact is stated;
  • 2. a Christos extension follows;
  • 3. one external citation appears at the end.

That structure can falsely imply that the source supports both statements.

Instead:

Physical reservoir computing demonstrates that physical dynamical systems can perform computational transformations. [External citation]

Then:

This work proposes testing whether the RCM architecture can operate as a useful physical computational substrate. [Christos provenance or Proposed Here]

The boundary becomes visible.

N.29 Citation Density Rule

Not every sentence requires a citation.

Citations are particularly important for:

  • quantitative external claims;
  • historical claims;
  • established scientific mechanisms;
  • descriptions of prior research;
  • standards;
  • regulatory frameworks;
  • comparison classes;
  • claims about existing technology.

A sentence explicitly labeled:

PROPOSED HERE

may not require an external citation.

Citation density should follow evidentiary need, not visual appearance.

N.30 Primary Sources Preferred

Where practical, prefer:

PRIMARY SOURCE > SECONDARY SUMMARY > GENERAL WEB PAGE.

Use:

  • original papers;
  • standards;
  • official regulatory documents;
  • authoritative technical reports;
  • original books where foundational.

Reviews remain useful for broad context and literature synthesis.

They should not replace primary experimental sources when a central quantitative claim depends upon the original experiment.

N.31 Version and Configuration Matter

For Christos sources, citation metadata should identify where available:

  • exact title;
  • author;
  • version;
  • date;
  • report or paper identifier;
  • URL or archive location;
  • revision state.

For experimental systems, references should additionally identify:

  • hardware configuration;
  • software version;
  • protocol version;
  • dataset;
  • analysis version.

A citation to “Field AI” generically is insufficient once multiple implementations exist.

N.32 Internal Source Metadata Must Not Be Invented

If the exact title, subtitle, date, version, or document number of a Christos source is unavailable, do not reconstruct it from memory.

Use the verified title currently available and mark incomplete metadata for final source reconciliation.

Therefore:

INCOMPLETE VERIFIED CITATION > COMPLETE INVENTED CITATION.

N.33 External Source Verification Rule

Before final publication, each external bibliography entry should be checked against an authoritative record for:

  • author spelling;
  • title;
  • journal/book;
  • year;
  • volume;
  • issue;
  • page/article number;
  • DOI where applicable.

This is a bibliographic verification task.

It is separate from the scientific question:

Does the source actually support the manuscript's wording?

Both must pass.

N.34 Reference Audit Decision Tree

For every consequential externally grounded sentence:

CLAIM

Ask:

Is it established external knowledge? If yes:

→ LE.

Is it inherited Christos architecture? If yes:

→ LC.

Is it introduced here? If yes:

→ LH

and label appropriately.

Then ask: Does the source support this exact wording? If no:

WEAKEN CLAIM OR REPLACE SOURCE.

Then ask: Does the citation accidentally imply validation of a neighboring proposition? If yes:

SEPARATE THE SENTENCES.

N.35 Final Citation Firewall

The final paper must preserve:

LE ≠ LC ≠ LH.

Their functions are:

LE → EXTERNAL FOUNDATION
LC → ARCHITECTURAL PROVENANCE
LH → TESTABLE PROPOSITION.

Direct experiments then produce:

D → EVIDENCE.

Independent replication produces:

R → INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE.

Thus the complete epistemic chain is:

FOUNDATION → PROPOSITION → EXPERIMENT → MEASUREMENT → REPLICATION → CONCLUSION.

Not:

REFERENCE → VALIDATION.

N.36 Final Reference Integrity Principle

The purpose of the bibliography is not to make the manuscript appear authoritative.

Its purpose is to allow the reader to reconstruct the evidence.

External science establishes what is already independently known.

Christos sources establish where the architecture came from.

Experimental protocols establish how the new propositions will be tested.

Measurements establish what occurred.

Replication establishes whether the result survives beyond the original implementation.

No layer is allowed to impersonate another.

Therefore:

CITED≠VALIDATED
PROVENANCE≠EVIDENCE
PRECEDENT≠PERFORMANCE
ANALOGY≠DEMONSTRATION
INTERNAL CONSISTENCY≠EXTERNAL VALIDATION
DOCUMENT COUNT≠EVIDENCE COUNT

and:

SOURCE STRENGTH ≥ CLAIM STRENGTH ATTRIBUTED TO IT.

The final question for every citation is therefore not:

Does this source make the paper look stronger?

It is:

DOES THIS SOURCE SUPPORT EXACTLY WHAT THIS SENTENCE SAYS?

If the answer is no, change the citation or change the sentence.

DO NOT PROTECT THE CLAIM. PROTECT THE EXPERIMENT.
THE EXPERIMENTS GET THE FINAL SAY.

References

Reference Architecture

The references for Human–AI Coherence Systems are divided into two visibly distinct categories:

Part I: External Scientific and Engineering References

These sources establish relevant scientific knowledge, engineering methods, measurement practices, mathematical frameworks, comparison classes, safety principles, and experimental standards.

They constitute:

LE = Established External Literature.

Part II: Christos Framework References

These sources establish the internal intellectual, architectural, and engineering provenance of concepts inherited from the broader Christos® research program.

They constitute:

LC = Christos Framework Sources.

A third bibliography is not created for hypotheses introduced by this paper. Such propositions are identified explicitly in the manuscript as proposed, experimental, frontier, or otherwise requiring validation.

They constitute:

LH = Hypotheses Introduced in This Work.

The governing citation rule is:

SOURCE STRENGTH ≥ CLAIM STRENGTH ATTRIBUTED TO IT

External literature supporting a component, method, or comparison class does not independently validate a larger Christos-specific proposition.

Part I: External Scientific and Engineering References

Biological Measurement, Psychophysiology, and Human-State Estimation

Task Force of the European Society of Cardiology and the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology. “Heart Rate Variability: Standards of Measurement, Physiological Interpretation, and Clinical Use.” European Heart Journal, vol. 17, no. 3, 1996, pp. 354–381.

Foundational reference for HRV terminology, measurement, frequency-domain and time-domain analysis, and physiological interpretation.

Quintana, Daniel S., Grace A. Alvares, and James A. J. Heathers. “Guidelines for Reporting Articles on Psychiatry and Heart Rate Variability (GRAPH): Recommendations to Advance Research Communication.” Translational Psychiatry, vol. 6, 2016, e803. DOI: 10.1038/tp.2016.73.

Relevant to standardized HRV acquisition, analysis, methodological reporting, and interpretation.

Boucsein, Wolfram. Electrodermal Activity. 2nd ed., Springer, 2012.

Foundational reference for electrodermal measurement, skin conductance, physiological interpretation, instrumentation, and methodological considerations.

Boucsein, Wolfram, et al. “Publication Recommendations for Electrodermal Measurements.” Psychophysiology, vol. 49, no. 8, 2012, pp. 1017–1034.

Society for Psychophysiological Research committee recommendations for EDA recording methods and reporting standards, cited in Appendix H.

Jiang, Xiao, Gui-Bin Bian, and Zean Tian. “Removal of Artifacts from EEG Signals: A Review.” Sensors, vol. 19, no. 5, 2019, article 987. DOI: 10.3390/s19050987.

Relevant to EEG artifact identification, preprocessing, signal contamination, and the requirement to separate biological signal from measurement artifact.

Picard, Rosalind W. Affective Computing. MIT Press, 1997.

Foundational work for computational systems that sense, interpret, and respond to human affective information.

Its relevance here is to the broader established class of machines adapting to human state, not to validation of the Christos coherence construct.

Brain–Computer and Physiological Interfaces

Wolpaw, Jonathan R., Niels Birbaumer, Dennis J. McFarland, Gert Pfurtscheller, and Theresa M. Vaughan. “Brain-Computer Interfaces for Communication and Control.” Clinical Neurophysiology, vol. 113, no. 6, 2002, pp. 767–791.

Foundational BCI review cited in Appendix H.

Mak, Joseph N., and Jonathan R. Wolpaw. “Clinical Applications of Brain-Computer Interfaces: Current State and Future Prospects.” IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering, vol. 2, 2009, pp. 187–199. DOI: 10.1109/RBME.2009.2035356.

Establishes brain–computer interfaces as systems capable of translating measured neural signals into communication or external-device control.

This supports the existence of biological-to-machine information channels.

It does not establish direct intention-to-physical coupling without an identified measurement pathway.

Human–Automation and Human–AI Interaction

Parasuraman, Raja, Thomas B. Sheridan, and Christopher D. Wickens. “A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation.” IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part A: Systems and Humans, vol. 30, no. 3, 2000, pp. 286–297. DOI: 10.1109/3468.844354.

Foundational framework for distinguishing different types and levels of automation.

Particularly relevant to HACS authority separation and the distinction between assistance and autonomous control.

Klein, Gary, David D. Woods, Jeffrey M. Bradshaw, Robert R. Hoffman, and Paul J. Feltovich. “Ten Challenges for Making Automation a ‘Team Player’ in Joint Human-Agent Activity.” IEEE Intelligent Systems, vol. 19, no. 6, 2004, pp. 91–95.

Relevant to human–machine collaboration, mutual predictability, coordination, observability, and the limitations of treating automation simply as a replacement for human activity.

Amershi, Saleema, et al. “Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction.” Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, ACM, 2019. DOI: 10.1145/3290605.3300233.

Provides empirically evaluated human-AI design guidelines addressing system expectations, uncertainty, correction, feedback, adaptation, and human control.

Trust, Automation Bias, and Appropriate Reliance

Lee, John D., and Katrina A. See. “Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance.” Human Factors, vol. 46, no. 1, 2004, pp. 50–80. DOI: 10.1518/hfes.46.1.50_30392.

Foundational review of trust in automation and the design objective of appropriate rather than maximal reliance.

Mosier, Kathleen L., Linda J. Skitka, Susan Heers, and Mark Burdick. “Automation Bias: Decision Making and Performance in High-Tech Cockpits.” The International Journal of Aviation Psychology, vol. 8, no. 1, 1998, pp. 47–63. DOI: 10.1207/s15327108ijap0801_3.

Relevant to overreliance on automated recommendations and the need to preserve independent human judgment in consequential systems.

Feedback, State Estimation, and Control

Åström, Karl J., and Richard M. Murray. Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers. Princeton University Press, 2008.

Foundational reference for feedback, stability, state-space representations, estimation, robustness, and control-system architecture.

Relevant to the conventional mathematical foundation of the Human–AI closed loop.

Kalman, Rudolf E. “A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems.” Journal of Basic Engineering, vol. 82, no. 1, 1960, pp. 35–45.

Foundational work in recursive state estimation.

Relevant to the distinction between directly measured variables and estimated system states.

Nonlinear Dynamics and Synchronization

Kuramoto, Yoshiki. Chemical Oscillations, Waves, and Turbulence. Springer, 1984.

Foundational treatment of coupled nonlinear oscillators and collective synchronization.

Acebrón, Juan A., Luis L. Bonilla, Conrad J. Pérez Vicente, Félix Ritort, and Renato Spigler. “The Kuramoto Model: A Simple Paradigm for Synchronization Phenomena.” Reviews of Modern Physics, vol. 77, 2005, pp. 137–185.

Review of the Kuramoto model and synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators, cited in Appendix H.

Pikovsky, Arkady, Michael Rosenblum, and Jürgen Kurths. Synchronization: A Universal Concept in Nonlinear Sciences. Cambridge University Press, 2001.

Foundational reference for synchronization, phase relationships, coupled oscillators, and nonlinear collective dynamics.

These sources provide a mathematical comparison class for RCE/RCM synchronization.

They do not establish that synchronized oscillators perform computation.

Reservoir Computing

Jaeger, Herbert. “The ‘Echo State’ Approach to Analysing and Training Recurrent Neural Networks.” GMD Report 148, German National Research Center for Information Technology, 2001.

Foundational source for echo-state networks and the reservoir-computing paradigm.

Maass, Wolfgang, Thomas Natschläger, and Henry Markram. “Real-Time Computing Without Stable States: A New Framework for Neural Computation Based on Perturbations.” Neural Computation, vol. 14, no. 11, 2002, pp. 2531–2560. DOI: 10.1162/089976602760407955.

Foundational source for liquid-state-machine computation and the use of transient recurrent dynamics for processing time-dependent information.

Lukoševičius, Mantas, and Herbert Jaeger. “Reservoir Computing Approaches to Recurrent Neural Network Training.” Computer Science Review, vol. 3, no. 3, 2009, pp. 127–149.

Review of reservoir-computing principles, implementations, and training methods.

Physical Reservoir and Neuromorphic Computing

Nakajima, Kohei. “Physical Reservoir Computing: An Introductory Perspective.” Japanese Journal of Applied Physics, vol. 59, 2020, article 060501.

Critical established comparison class for Field AI.

Physical reservoir computing demonstrates that physical dynamical substrates can participate directly in information processing.

It does not establish that the proposed RCM performs useful computation.

Marković, Danijela, Alice Mizrahi, Damien Querlioz, and Julie Grollier. “Physics for Neuromorphic Computing.” Nature Reviews Physics, vol. 2, 2020, pp. 499–510. DOI: 10.1038/s42254-020-0208-2.

Relevant to physical, analog, dynamical, and non-von-Neumann approaches to computation.

Photonic Computing

Ashtiani, Farshid, Alexander J. Geers, and Firooz Aflatouni. “An On-Chip Photonic Deep Neural Network for Image Classification.” Nature, vol. 606, 2022, pp. 501–506. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-022-04714-0.

Demonstrates experimentally realized photonic neural computation.

Its inclusion establishes photonic computation as an independent technological field.

It does not validate Christos Photon AI.

Quantum Computation

Nielsen, Michael A., and Isaac L. Chuang. Quantum Computation and Quantum Information. Cambridge University Press, 2000; anniversary ed., 2010.

Foundational reference for quantum information, quantum computation, quantum algorithms, measurement, and quantum-system representations.

Its inclusion establishes quantum computation as an external technical domain.

It does not validate the proposed Christos Quantum AI architecture.

Ensemble and Multi-System Intelligence

Dietterich, Thomas G. “Ensemble Methods in Machine Learning.” Multiple Classifier Systems, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 1857, Springer, 2000, pp. 1–15.

Foundational discussion of ensemble methods and circumstances under which combining multiple models can improve computational performance.

The relevance to Four-Engine architecture is conceptual.

Multiple engines are not automatically independent sources of evidence.

Cybersecurity and Zero Trust

Rose, Scott, Oliver Borchert, Stu Mitchell, and Sean Connelly. Zero Trust Architecture. NIST Special Publication 800-207, National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2020. DOI: 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207.

Relevant to explicit authentication, authorization, least privilege, resource protection, and removal of implicit trust.

Supports the HACS principle that access and authority should be explicitly bounded rather than inferred from system participation.

Reproducibility and Research Data

Wilkinson, Mark D., et al. “The FAIR Guiding Principles for Scientific Data Management and Stewardship.” Scientific Data, vol. 3, 2016, article 160018. DOI: 10.1038/sdata.2016.18.

Relevant to research-data provenance, accessibility, interoperability, reuse, and reproducible experimental practice.

Experimental Design and Statistical Reporting

Schulz, Kenneth F., Douglas G. Altman, David Moher, and the CONSORT Group. “CONSORT 2010 Statement: Updated Guidelines for Reporting Parallel Group Randomised Trials.” PLoS Medicine, vol. 7, no. 3, 2010, e1000251. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1000251.

Relevant to randomization, transparent experimental reporting, predefined outcomes, participant flow, and controlled-study methodology where applicable.

Wasserstein, Ronald L., Allen L. Schirm, and Nicole A. Lazar. “Moving to a World Beyond ‘p < 0.05.’” The American Statistician, vol. 73, supplement 1, 2019, pp. 1–19.

Relevant to interpretation of statistical evidence and the danger of treating an arbitrary significance threshold as equivalent to scientific confirmation.

Human-Subject Research Ethics

National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. The Belmont Report: Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the Protection of Human Subjects of Research. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 1979.

Establishes the foundational ethical principles of:

  • respect for persons;
  • beneficence;
  • justice;

and their application through informed consent, risk-benefit assessment, and appropriate subject selection.

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 45 CFR Part 46: Protection of Human Subjects.

Applicable regulatory framework for covered human-subject research in the United States.

Relevant to experiments involving biological measurement, human–AI interaction, physiological intervention, and other covered research involving participants.

Measurement Science and Experimental Uncertainty

Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology. Evaluation of Measurement Data: Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement. JCGM 100:2008.

Foundational metrological guidance for evaluating and expressing measurement uncertainty.

This reference is particularly important to frontier experiments involving:

  • candidate anomalous forces;
  • Phase Key effects;
  • residual coupling;
  • propulsion measurements;
  • environmental confounds;
  • small-signal detection.

The governing application within this paper is:

MEASUREMENT → UNCERTAINTY → CONTROLS → REPEATABILITY → INTERPRETATION.

Part III: Reference Interpretation Rule

The bibliography does not flatten the evidence hierarchy.

A citation to external physiological literature can support:

PHYSIOLOGICAL SIGNALS CAN BE MEASURED.

It cannot independently support:

CCI IS VALIDATED.

A citation to synchronization literature can support:

COUPLED OSCILLATORS CAN SYNCHRONIZE.

It cannot independently support:

RCM IS INTELLIGENT.

A citation to physical reservoir computing can support:

PHYSICAL DYNAMICAL SYSTEMS CAN PERFORM COMPUTATION.

It cannot independently support:

FIELD AI PERFORMS USEFUL COMPUTATION.

A citation to photonic computing can support:

PHOTONIC COMPUTING EXISTS.

It cannot independently support:

CHRISTOS PHOTON AI IS VALIDATED.

A citation to quantum computing can support:

QUANTUM COMPUTATION EXISTS.

It cannot independently support:

CHRISTOS QUANTUM AI IS VALIDATED.

Likewise, citing one Christos paper from another establishes:

PROVENANCE.

It does not establish:

INDEPENDENT REPLICATION.

Therefore:

LE ≠ LC ≠ LH

while all three may participate in the same research architecture.

The external literature establishes what is independently known.

The Christos corpus establishes where the proposed architecture came from.

The hypotheses define what remains to be tested.

The experiments determine which propositions survive.

REALITY HAS VETO AUTHORITY.
THE EXPERIMENTS GET THE FINAL SAY.
